[Hindu] In Hindu mythology, the heavens and city of Brahma. It is situated on the summit of Mount Meru.

[Other] The herb of oblivion in Melanesia. It is given to the souls of the dead when they arrive in Tuma (Paradise). Its fragrance is so strong that the souls will forget all about their previous existence on earth and they will live happily ever after.
[Other] In Malay cosmology, Bukit Kaca is the Mountain of Glass. It is so high that its summit reflects the rays of the rising sun so that we see it red, orange, and amber.
[Celtic] A continental Celtic god, identified with Jupiter.
[Other] An evil spirit, the opposite of Agathodemon (a good spirit).
[Roman] The wet nurse of Aeneas. She was buried at the place of the same name (currently Gaeta) in Latium.
[Folklore] "Hard-belly". A legendary Irish sword, capable of consuming everything.
[Arthurian] South-western Welsh town. Claims to be the birthplace of Merlin and derives it's name from him. The opposite is true - "Myrddin" is a derivation of the Roman name Moridunum.
[Roman] The Roman goddess associated with the bodily organs, particularly the heart. Carna's festival was observed on June 1.
[Celtic] A Celtic war god of Britain.
[Greek] Three giants with a hundred arms each. See Hecatonchires.
[Aztec] An Aztec god of the underworld.
[Hindu] A Hindu goddess. A form of Durgha and one of the nine navadurgas.
[Hindu] A Hindu god; a benevolent aspect of Shiva, whom he serves.
[Hindu] A Hindu goddess. A form of Durgha and one of the nine navadurgas.
[Etruscan] Etruscan demons of death. The name suggests a connection to the Greek Charon and his Etruscan equivalent Charun.
[Hindu] "Shadow". A Hindu goddess; a reflection of the goddess Sanjna. She was the consort of Surya and the mother of Sani.
[Other] The inhabitants of the underworld in Siberian myth. They are composed mainly of iron and are black in color and are not particularly friendly towards human beings.
[Other] The work god of the Chibcha Indians
[Native American] The sky and wolf-spirit of the Algonquin. Chibiabos is the lord of the realm of the spirits. He is a brother of the Great Hare Manabozho.
[Aztec] The Aztec hearth-goddess, and guardian of the household.
[Japanese] An area-related kami. A kami, worshipped by a small group living in a particular geographical area, which protects that area.
[Other] A monkey-gifl from the Filipino Tagalog tale. Prince Pedro was forced to marry her for fear of being bewitched by her mother. In the end she was changed into a lovely princess.
[Greek heroic] The son of Pelops and Axioche. He was killed by his stepbrothers Atreus and Thyestes.
[Chinese] The king of the second of the Taoist hells, the hell of thieves and murderers. It is believed to be a large lake of ice. Chu Jiang is honored on the first day of the Third Moon.

[Japanese] Sun goddess of the Ainu peoples. Originally she was the moon goddess but after one night overhead watching all the adulterous behavings below she begged the sun god to trade places with her; he did.
[Aztec] "Star Garment". An Aztec creator goddess. She is the consort of Citlalatonac, and together they created the stars.
[Roman] The Roman goddess of mercy and clemency.
[Native American] The incident of a monster kicking people over a cliff so that they may be eaten by her brood occurs in many North American Indian tales.
[Greek heroic] A friend of Patroclus, who killed him during a quarrel.
[Aztec] The Aztec god of merchants and commerce.
[Folklore] The Danish giant slain by Guy of Warwick. By his death the land was delivered from Danish tribute.
[Other] The spirits of people who have died of smallpox in Annamese belief. The victims are kept isolated for fear of the Con ma dau which are residing in their bodies.
[Celtic] Conchobar's intended bride, Deirdre, eloped with Noيse. Conchobar killed Noisi and his brothers and Deridre died of sorrow.
[Celtic] A local god in the area of Lancaster in Celto-Roman Britain.

[Celtic] The Celtic (Britain) goddess of water and springs. She was known locally in the area of Carrawburgh (Roman Brocolitia) along Hadrian's Wall. She personified a holy spring that had healing powers.
[Celtic] A Welsh goddess, daughter of Llyr. She appeared in Shakespeare's King Lear as the king's daughter Cordelia.
[Celtic] This entry is currently under revision.
[Greek] Another name for Hermes. So called from Mount Cyllene, in Peloponnesus, where he was born.
[Greek heroic] The son of Telephus. He possessed a deer that was given to him by Apollo. When he accidentally killed the animal he became inconsolable and the god turned him into a cypress.
[Greek heroic] The father of Chione. Driven by sadness over his daughter's death he threw himself of the Parnassus and was changed into a hawk by Apollo.
[Native American] Mythical animals who appear in dreams, visions, and temporal reality and have the ability to take on many forms.

[Japanese] The Japanese Great bodhisattva, the Buddha-Elect or the Buddha in his previous world appearance. A gigantic statue of the meditating Buddha as world ruler can be found near Kamakura and is called Daibutsu.
[Mesopotamian] The Mesopotamian mother-goddess, consort of the god Enki. She is often identified with the Sumerian earth-goddess Ninchursanga. Her Akkadian equivalent is Damkina (spouse of Ea).
[Haitian] The Haitian loa of farmers. He originated from the African god Danh.

[Folklore] The spirit or personification of the sea in sailors' lingo. Davy Jones's locker is the bottom of the sea. To go to Davy Jones's Locker is a common phrase meaning to be drowned at sea, or to die and be buried at sea.
[Roman] The 'silent goddess'. A Roman goddess of dead. (See also Larenta.)
[Folklore] A tinkling in the ears, supposed by the Scottish peasantry to announce the death of a friend.
[Roman] The Roman gods of profit. In time they were superceded by Mercury.
[Greek heroic] The son of Priam and Hecuba. After Paris' death he married Helen. During Troy's downfall he was killed by Menelaus.
[Greek] An epithet of Dionysus as fertility-god, literally meaning "he of the trees."

[Other] The rice goddess of Bali. Goddess of both the underworld and the moon, she has both earthly and celestial powers. Although she rules life, through her control of the foodstuffs of the earth, she also controls death, which returns us to her bosom.
[Hindu] Another Hindu goddess of misfortune, a malevolent nakshatra. She is a daughter of Daksha and consort of Chandra (Soma).
[Other] The primary goddess of the Arabs of Yemen. She was a goddess of the natural forces of the wilderness, worshiped especially in tree-circled oases.
[Hindu] A Hindu goddess. She is one of the ten mahavidyas personifying the Sakti of Shiva.
[Chinese] The Ruler of the Earth in religious Taoism. One of the three San-guan. He plays an important part in the religious life of the Chinese. Di-guan forgives sins and transgressions.

[Celtic] The daughter of the sun in ancient Scotland. She appears in a folktale in which, held captive in the Land of the Big Women, she is freed by the Cailleach, disguised as a fox, and a helpful young bumbler named Brian.
[Haitian] In Haitian religion, a loa of European origin. He is feared for his great severity.
[Other] The Buddha who is regarded as the first predecessor of the original Buddha. He is very popular in Nepal. In China he is called Ran Deng Fo. His name means "he who lights the lamps".
[Roman] The personified Roman goddess of strife and discord. She belonged to the retinue of Mars and Bellona. She is the Greek Eris.
[Roman] The Roman god of oaths. Dius Fidus is of Sabine origin.
[Native American] A group of people with power, creators and culture heroes, often referred to as the Holy People. Similar to the Apache hactin.

[Aboriginal] The divine trinity of north Australian mythology, Djanggawuls was made up of two sisters and a brother who came to Earth via Beralku, the island of the dead, and gave the landscape its shape and vegetation.
[Roman] The Roman god who guides a bride to her new home.
[Other] The wife of the Domovoi. She lived in the cellers of houses while her husband lived in the household stove.
[Aboriginal] The mythological past of Australian (Aboriginal) mythology. It is variously termed by the various tribes. More to come...
[Other] A blind king in Javanese mythology, the father of the Korawas. He is the son of Abiasa and Ambiki.
[Other] An important goddess in Siberia; she ruled over the clan territory.
[Hindu] In Hindu mythology and religion, a malignant form of Devi, the inaccessible, represented by a yellow woman riding a tiger. Also Kali or Parvati. She is the consort of Shiva.
[Native American] The Frog Princess of Haida mythology, she is also referred to as the Volcano Woman, who arrived from the sea with six canoe-loads of people. Her husband was Kaiti, the bear god.
[Other] This Polish Goddess was matron of spring and agriculture. She was especially honored by farmers.
[Greek] The female personification of a Greek ritual object: a branch of olive wood, twined with wool and hung with fruits, which was carried in festivals by children with two living parents
[Native American] The earth. Her name means "our mother".
[Japanese] The Japanese god of epidemic diseases such as plague and pestilence.
[Greek heroic] The son of Perseus and Andromeda. He was the king of Mycene and father of Alcmene.

[Greek] One of the hundred-armed Gigantes. He fought against the Olympians, and Zeus hit him with a bolt of lightning and locked him beneath Mt. Aetna, which shook each time he rolled over to his other side.
[Mesopotamian] With Nindukugga, Sumerian gods living in the underworld; parents of Enlil.

[Mesopotamian] The Sumerian god of the underworld. He is "lord of all mes" (the powers on which civilization and society are based on, the divine laws). His wife is Ninmesarra, "mistress of all humans".
[Mesopotamian] The temple of the moon-god in Sumerian Ur.
[Mesopotamian] A river in the nether world.

[Greek heroic] The father of Antinous. When his son, the most aggressive of Penelope's suitors, was killed by Odysseus, he tried to raise the people of Ithaca against Odysseus. He was, however, killed by Laertes.
[Greek heroic] A herald in the Greek army before Troy.
[Greek heroic] The king of Mycene, son of Sthenelus. By Hera's cunning, Heracles was for a long time subservient to Eurystheus. During that time he performed the so-called 'Twelve Labors'.

[Roman] A minor Roman god of infants. Mentioned by Varro, Fabulinus taught Roman children to utter their first word. He received an offering when the child spoke its first words. (From fabulari, to speak.)
[Native American] Fas-ta-chee is the name of a small anthropomorphic dwarf also know as "Little Give(er)" and is a lower level provider figure of corn and medicine. Also Es-te-fas-ta (-chee?).
[Roman] The goddess who protects the herds.

[Roman] In Roman myth, the shepherd who found the twins Romulus and Remus on the Palentine Hill where they were reared by a she-wolf. He took them with him and gave them to his wife Acca Larentia to raise.
[Roman] The Roman personification of success. Her temples were closely associated with the person of the emperor and one was located on the Forum Romanum.

[Chinese] The Chinese goddess of the winds, literally "Madam Wind". She is represented as an old, wrinkled woman, sitting on a tiger riding on a path made of clouds. On quiet days she placed the winds back in the bag she carries over her shoulder.
[Chinese] The Chinese phoenix and the personification of the primordial force of the heavens. Feng-huang has the head and the comb of a pheasant and the tail of a peacock.
[Roman] The goddess of the mountain city of Ferentinum in Latium. She was protector of the Latin commonwealth.
[Folklore] A female of the Gremlin family who tickled fighter pilots and bombardiers just as their sights were lined up for a good run.
[Celtic] In Irish legend, the daughter of Lir, who was transformed into a swan and condemned to wander over the lakes and rivers until Christianity came to Ireland.
[Folklore] The Fir Darrig is a malevolent elf and fond of playing rather nasty tricks. He is best left alone.

[Native American] Small with pointed ears, they are always seen or encountered in mated pairs traversing North and South paths, never easterly-westerly. They are seen most frequently at the headwaters of streams and creeks.
[Native American] A human empowered to bring rain, turn stone, and can cure sickness.
[Persian] "Making wonderful." In Persian mythology, restoring to goodness: the dead will be restored to life at the end of time by Astvat-Ereta.

[Folklore] Subject of a medieval local legend of the Tyrol, built around a certain rock which resembles a woman. This rock is said to be Frau Hütt, a woman of that locality who was turned to stone for wasting food.
[Folklore] The name that was given to the female supernatural paramour or fairy mistress of general European folk belief by medieval clerics; and according to them, the Devil.

[Japanese] The Japanese Shinto god of wisdom, luck and longevity. He is one of the seven god of luck (the Shichi Fukujin). He is depicted with a very high forehead (nearly equal to the length of his body), accompanied by a turtle and a crow.

[Greek heroic] A servant of Alcmene. When Hera tried to prevent the birth of Heracles, Galanthis deceived Hera with the news that Alcmene had already given birth. Hera punished her by turning the unfortunate woman into a weasel.

[Greek] One of the Nereids, and the beloved of Acis, a Sicilian shepherd. She was also loved by Polyphemus, who killed Acis with a boulder in jealousy. From his blood, Galatea created the river Acis on Sicily.
[Persian] A Persian water-demon who continually tries to devour the good things of creation. Eventually he will be defeated by the hero Keresaspa.
[Chinese] The ancient Chinese god of judgment. On his quest for injustice he is accompanied by a ram. He is also known as Ting-jian.
[Folklore] The great dragon that lived in the river Seine (France) and which ravaged Rouen. It was slain in the 7th century by the Archbishop of Rouen, St. Romanus.
[Other] In the Javanese wayang myths, a formidable warrior who posesses a magic jacket with which he can fly long distances. He is the son of Bima by the giantess Arimbi.
[Persian] The first man or first mortal ancestor. The word comes from the old Persian gayo, "life", and maretan, which means "mortal".
[Arthurian] A knight of King Arthur's court.
[Folklore] The Ghillie Dhu is a solitary Scottish elf who lives in birches. His clothes are woven from leaves and moss.
[Native American] The Penobscot variant of Glooskap.
[Chinese] A Chinese demon who is responsible for the great floods, together with his associate, the snake-like Xiang Yao. Gong Gong is the eternal opponent of the highest ruler.
[Japanese] A Japanese mountain deity, an incarnated living spirit, a Shinto incarnation of the Buddha. Mountain climbers hope to gain enlightenment on the mountain which have such a spirit.
[Basque] Reddish spirits of Basque folklore that run very rapidly on some mountains.
[Folklore] The name for amulets and charms in Africa. A greegree man is one who sells these amulets.

[Haitian] In voodoo-religion, Guinee is the legendary place of origin and abode of the gods. It is here that the souls of the deceased go after their death. On their way to Guinee, they first have to pass the eternal crossroads which is guarded by Ghede.

[Other] The son of Guriang Tunggal, the supreme god, and Ambu Dewi. He lives on earth as Luting Kasarung, the Black Monkey, to protect princess Purba Sari against the whims of her wicked elder sister the queen.

[Arthurian] Hero of Welsh legend found in Culhwch and Olwen, the triads and other sources. He is courteous and eloquent in addition to being a brave warrior. He is seen as the nephew of Arthur and is equated often with Gawain.
[Native American] The Tlingit and Haida tribes of Alaska considered her a beneficent forest goddess.
[Mayan] The Lacandon Maya god of real people. People who were not Lacandon Maya were not considered to be real persons.
[Folklore] A field spirit from German folklore. The name means "oat goat".
[Hindu] In Hindu myth, an appellation of Devi as born of the Himalaya mountains.
[Other] The Teutonic winter-king, represented with raven wings.
[Greek] Tree nymphs who lived and died with the tree they inhabited.
[Other] A Malaysian water-spirit or ghost. The phosphorescence of the sea is attributed to him.
[Other] The tutelary deity of the Hittite throne. The king receives from her his right to rule.
[Arthurian] A French verse translation from the mid-twelfth century of the Historia Regum Britanniae by Geoffrey of Monmouth. Extant in five fragments, it ends before Arthur's battle with Rome.

[Greek heroic] A Thracian princes who was raised by her father, King Harpalycus, as an amazon. She excelled especially in sprinting and running (Virgil I, 317). After her death she was venerated as a divine being.
[Islamic] The great-grandfather of the Prophet Muhammad. He is the ancestor of the kings of Transjordan. He was very hospitable, hence the name Hashim.
[Norse] "Orb of the World." An important collection of sixteen sagas on the lives of the early kings of Norway, up to 1184. It is the work of Snorri Sturluson (1179-1241) who also wrote the Edda.
[Other] "Book of Heroes", the name of a collection of 13th-century German epic poety. It contains various stories which are based on national sagas. Dietrich von Bern is a central figure in the book.
[Judaic] The first six books of the Bible. It comprises Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy and Joshua.
[Greek heroic] The son of Oebalus, brother of Tyndareos. He drove his son from Sparta and seized power himself, until he was killed by Heracles.

[Greek heroic] The wife of Pirithous. At their wedding the battle between the Centaurs and the Lapiths began. The daughter of Oenomaus and Asterope. By Pelops she became the mother of Atreus, Thyestes, and Alcathous.
[Greek heroic] The son of Poseidon and Alope. After the death of Cercyon he ruled of Eleusis.
[Other] The village guardian of the Wild Wa (Burma). The Wa live in terror of this nat and post the spoils of the head-hunting expeditions in order to propriate him.
[Norse] One of the Valkyries. Hladgunnr used to set traps for her victims.
[Egyptian] A variation of the Egyptian god Horus.
[Other] The ancient Lapp god of thunder. He is usually portrayed carrying two hammers (the symbol of thunder). His wife is the goddess Raudni. He is equated with the Norse god Thor.
[Japanese] The Japanese cuckoo. The bird has a sad cry, which is explained by the country people as the melancholy longing of a dead soul to return to the land of her loved ones.
[Chinese] A Chinese guardian god, one of the Men-shen. He was originally a general from the Tang Dynasty.
[Folklore] Small Hungarian being that lives in moors and swamps.
[Islamic] Abdullah, son of Abbas, and so a cousin of Muhammad, to whom Jibril explained the Qur'an. He became the ancestor of the Abbasids.
[Native American] Literally, great tellings. The long migration myths and war tales of the Mohave Indians.
[Islamic] "Inspiration of the heart", as received by the saints of Islam.
[Roman] The Roman god of the third ploughing. See also Redarator and Vervactor.
[Roman] The Roman gods of the underworld.
[Basque] The Lord of Dreams in Basque mythology, he is malevolent and mostly known for sneaking into the houses at night to send nightmares and molest the inhabitants.
[African] A female spirit of the Zulus who makes the maize grow. The deity of agriculture, she is venerated in springtime.
[Other] One of two proto-Hattic goddesses of fate. With a distaff and a mirror they determine the fate of humans. The other goddess is Papaya.
[Mesopotamian] The gardener of Anu, who presented baskets of dates to Anu's daugther Ishtar, whom he loved. She however, turned him into a frog after making love to him.
[Japanese] In Japanese mythology, a sage or priest of one inch in height. He traveled on water in a rice bowl, paddling with a chopstick. He defeated two demons with a needle.
[Mayan] One of the thirteen Maya gods who created human beings.
[Aztec] The Aztec god of healing and medicine, as well as feasting and games.
[Hindu] The Hindu 'World-mother', another name for Durgha.

[Folklore] These seasonal faeries are found in Mexico and Central America. They resemble pudgy children with wings and aid in the turning of the Wheel Of the Year. Males are Jimaninos, females are Jimaninas.

[Judaic] "Dove". The son of Amittai. He was commissioned to denounce Nineveh. His book is the 32nd of the Old Testament and the 5th of the minor prophets. In it he narrates his refusal, escape from drowning, final acceptance and successful ministry.
[Japanese] The Japanese Buddhist god of mercy.
[Polynesian] One of the two lizard women who keep the soul of the deceased imprisoned. The other one is Kilioa.
[Other] Ancient Finnish magic songs and lyrics. They are of the type called runos, some of which are preserved in the Kalevala.

[Other] One of the four most prominent gods of the Singhalese pantheon. He is depicted with six heads and his mount is a peacock. He is closely related to the young Tamil god Murukan and the Hindu god Skanda.
[Native American] The solar deity of the Abenaki. He is an eagle who opens his wings to create the day, and closes them to create the night. Kee-zos-en is a being from the so-called Ancient Age.
[Native American] A snake-spirit who fights the thunder and lightning spirits Pa-don-gi-ak.

[Other] A Celtic saint of the 5th century. She was the daughter of Brychan, the King of Brecknock. St. Keyne's Well, situated near Liskeard in Cornwall, is reputed to give the upper hand to the first of the marriage partners to drink from it.
[Native American] In Eskimo myth, a fanged demon and the enemy of priests.
[Polynesian] The supreme god of the people of the Tuamotu archipelago southeast of Tahiti.
[Japanese] The national flower of Japan. The symbol on the Japanese flag, a rising sun, was originally a kiku, a chrysanthemum, with sixteen petals.
[Japanese] The Japanese goddess of luck and of beauty. She is the patroness of song and dance, protectress of the geishas. She is the sister of the war god Bishamon.
[Mayan] The Mayan god of earthquakes, often taken to be another form of the god of the underworld Cizin.
[Japanese] In Japanese cosmology, the Buddhist Vajra-Dhatu, the Diamond-Element, the Essence of Wisdom. The name means "Diamond-Wonder".
[Folklore] A German field spirit, the spirit of the growing grain incarnate in the last sheaf.
[Hindu] The six Pleiades, fosterers of the six-headed war-god Karttikeya.
[Chinese] Cantonese. The zombies of Chinese myth (see: Geong Si).
[Folklore] A different name for dragon-like creature Bolla from Albanian folklore.
[Other] The god of fate of the Tontemboan people.
[Japanese] The Japanese god of rain and snow.
[Other] The beneficent raven god of the Siberian Koryak people. He taught mankind the art of fishing, hunting, and making fire. He also gave them the drums shamans use.
[Haitian] A Haitian loa who lives among rocks and ravines. He is said to kill those who offend him.
[Greek heroic] The descendants of Labdacus, among which Laius, Oedipus, Eteocles, Polynices, etc.
[Polynesian] In Tongan myth, the ruler of the winds. He was sent down to earth by his father Tamapo.
[Other] One of three patron deities of the field. The others are Datan and Tawals.
[Celtic] A Continental Celtic god of thunder.
[Greek] The king of Messinia, father of Phoebe and Hilaera. His daughters were abducted by the Dioscuri.

[Greek] The beloved of Helios. She was betrayed by Clytia and her father buried her alive. After her death she turned into an incense-plant. Leucothea is also the name of Ino as a marine-deity, which see.
[Greek heroic] The son of Electryon. He accompanied Heracles on many of his journeys.
[Other] A mysterious plant in Malay mythology. If a person holds the plant to his ear, he can hear the earth (Bumi) talk. And the earth knows everything, even the future.
[Other] The first woman in the mythology of the Marshall Islands.
[Chinese] The Transcendental Official, and the guardian of the palace of Yu-huang. He was so widely venerated that a separate temple was dedicated to him in Beijing (Peking) in the 15th century.
[Other] Dwarfs, or dwarf-like spirits, from the New Hebrides who live in trees or stones. If a man offends them they will devour him.
[Greek heroic] The son of the Phrygian king Midas. He challenged every guest to a contest in harvesting. Those he conquered he beheaded, until he was killed himself by Heracles.
[Native American] A cannibal clown, also called Hagondes.
[Other] One of the four major world cataclysms in the mythology of the Chaco and Tierra del Fuego Indians of South America.
[Polynesian] The abode of the dead in the Polynesian Land of the Dead. Literally, "Milu's Cave".
[Greek heroic] The king of the Dolopes on the island Skyros. Achilles remained there for some time, and became the father of Neoptolemus by Lycomedes' daughter Deidamea.
[Mayan] "The Distinguished Name". The third Man created by Hurakan from white and yellow maize paste, after he flooded the world.
[Roman] The goddess of whom the month of May is probably named after. Offerings were made to her in this month. She is associated with Vulcan and sometimes equated with Fauna and Ops.
[Other] The most clever and powerful of the Twins in the mythology of various Carib tribes of the Guianas. He often plays the part of culture hero.
[Inca] The harvest and earth goddess from Inca mythology. She was usually portrayed with many breasts, which indicates fertility and the nourishing powers of the earth.
[Inca] The Inca goddess of the sea, and provider of all the fish from the sea. She is the favorite of fishermen and mariners. The supreme god Viracocha is her husband. Her name means "Sea Mother".
[Inca] The Inca mother goddess, and daughter of the sun god Inti and the moon goddess Mama_Quilla. She taught her children (the Incas) the art of spinning.

[Inca] Mama Pacha was the Earth Mother of the Chincha of Peru. She oversees planting and harvesting. Some depict her as a great dragon who causes earthquakes. The supreme god Pachacamac emerged from her. She is also mentioned as his consort.

[Aboriginal] In Aboriginal belief, Mamaragan is the man of lightning who rides on a thundercloud and who throws bolts of lightning to men and trees. Thunder is his voice. During good weather he lives in a puddle.
[Other] One of the ten types of Filipino witches, the Managtanem uses a type of magic called Kulam, similar to voodoo of the Caribbean. Managtanem frequently use a "voodoo doll".
[Polynesian] Heavenly nymphs in Polynesian cosmology, the attendants of Io the Creator. They act as messengers to earth and guardians of souls.
[Folklore] The hero of a sequence of Danish ballads. He was a champion of the people against Eric, a tyrannous king.
[Hindu] The sun in Vedic mythology. He is the son of Aditi by the sun; her eight son, whom she cast away, one of the Adityas.
[Other] The Melanesian god who created females. The Papuans he taught how to make longhouses.
[Other] Greek form of Miriam. The betrothed of Joseph and mother of Christ.
[Folklore] Female demon of lust in Cantabria (northern Spain) mythology.
[Polynesian] The Polynesian East Wind. It was the third of the winds to be brought under control by Maui. Another name for the East Wind is Marangai.
[Hindu] The Vedic messenger of the gods.

[Native American] The creator deity of the Kamaiura Indians, who turned a shell into a woman and begot a son, the first man. Then Mavutsinim took away the child and the tearful mother went to a lagoon, returning to a shell again
[Other] The Lithuanian god of animals and the forest.
[Greek heroic] The son of Dolius, and shepherd of Odysseus.
[Greek heroic] The name for the sisters of Meleager. After his death they mourned for him constantly, and Artemis turned them into guinea hens.
[Greek] A legendary king of Crete, father of the nymph Melissa.
[Greek heroic] The father of Creon and Jocasta.
[Other] The King of Moab who triumphed over the Israelites (2 Kings 3:4), whereupon he erected an inscribed stone, dedicated to the god Chemosh, as a thanks-giving.
[Egyptian] An Egyptian goddess who acted as a midwife and who presided over the birth-chamber. She accompanied the goddess Renenet (Fortune).
[Latvian] The Latvian god of forests. Rather obscure and little used. Mentioned by Paul Einhorn, may be a substitute for the word "wolf" - vilks used to avoid invoking the beast.
[Other] The goddess of the underworld in Niquiran mythology.
[Native American] Glooskap's older brother and the focus of the Malisset tales.
[Japanese] In Japanese Buddhism, the doctrine that purification ceremonies are periodically needed to cleanse the self of lust and anger.
[Other] The Spider. In South Carolina Sea Island folk tale, a corruption of Anansi.
[Greek heroic] A Trojan, one of the companions of Odysseus on his journeys.
[Celtic] A Welsh goddess, daughter of Avalloc, derived from the Celtic goddess Matrona. She is regarded as a prototype of Morgan (from Arthurian Legend).

[Celtic] The one-eyed Celtic/Irish god of the sun who rides through the sky in a shining bronze chariot, or who flies through the sky like a bird. The word ruith is possibly derived from the Irish roth, meaning "wheel" (representing the sun).
[Native American] The Abenaki mink-spirit. He is the adopted son of Gluskab and a powerful fletcher. Occasionally he fulfills wishes.

[Hindu] In Buddhist mythology and belief, the serpent-king. He spread his hood as a canopy over Buddha to shelter him from the elements during the third week of the period preceding the enlightenment.
[Polynesian] In Fijian mythology, Murimuria is a sort of Purgatory. Here the souls receive either rewards or punishment.
[Greek] "Leader of the Muses". An epithet of Apollo as leader of the nine Muses.
[Polynesian] The village of souls in the Fijian Land of the Dead.
[Native American] Nagi Tanka, most often accepted to be translated as Great Spirit or Great Mystery, is one of the other names for the Creator. Also known as Taku Skanskan.

[Folklore] An Argentinian lake monster. Like its counterpart Nessie, it too is named after the lake it supposedly inhabits, the Nahuel Huapi Lake. Descriptions of the appearance of the creature vary rather, as does those of its size.
[Folklore] "Red dwarf". A lutin of house spirit of Normandy, kind to fishermen. There is another called le petit homme rouge (the little red man).
[Japanese] A Japanese goddess, born from the tears of Izanagi when he mourned for his dead wife.
[Hindu] In Hindu myth, the stars, the divine attendants upon Indra.
[Native American] Nanabozho (also Wenabozho) is the trickster hare of the Ojibwa (Chippewa).
[Aztec] The Aztec god who sacrificed himself in a fire so that the sun should continue to shine over the world.
[Other] The man-lion, fourth incarnation of Vishnu.
[Greek heroic] The son of Odysseus and Calypso, or according to others, of Odysseus and Circe.
[Greek] The son of Poseidon and Periboea. He was the king of the Phaeacians and settled with his people on Scheria, where later his son Alcinous ruled.
[Roman] Necessitas ("necessity") is a Roman goddess of destiny. She is similar to the Greek Ananke.
[Other] "The Goddess". In Kiribati myth, she is the daughter of Na Atibu and Nei Teuke, the first beings.
[Other] In Kiribati myth, the first woman. She was created by the spider-god Nareau. With the first man Na Atibu she procreated the gods.
[African] A mythical culture hero of the Masai (Africa).
[Roman] A Roman god of the woods.
[Other] "People's victor". The Pharisee ruler and timid convert who assisted at Christ's sepulture.
[Mesopotamian] A Sumerian local goddess of Isin (an important Sumerian settlement).
[Mesopotamian] With Endukugga, parental gods living in the underworld.
[Mesopotamian] The Babylonian goddess of the books of the dead.

[Mesopotamian] A fertility god, addressed as 'Lord of the Tree of Life'. Sometimes he is a serpent with a human head, but later he was a god of healing and magic. He is the companion of Tammuz with whom he stood at the gate of heaven.
[Mesopotamian] The Babylonian and Sumerian goddess of healing who nursed sick humans.

[Other] The national god of Elam, in ancient Asia Minor, and the tutelary deity of Susa, the country's capital. He is also the god of the oath and the judge of the dead. His consort is Pinikir. His Akkadian name is Susinak.
[Mesopotamian] A Mesopotamian goddess. She is an aspect of Belet-Ili, mother of the gods.
[Native American] The Eskimo god of icebergs.
[Roman] The Roman appellation of the nine great gods of the Etruscans.

[Other] The god of the heavens of the Voguls (Mansi) of Siberia. He dwells in the highest heaven and lives in a house littered with gold and silver. He has seven sons and many assistant spirits. Among the Ostyaks he was called Num-Turem.
[Japanese] The god of the crater of Mount Fuji.
[African] An Yoruban earth deity, also known as Shakpono. His name means "Master of the Universe" (i.e. the Earth). His equivalents are the Dahomean Sagbata and the Ashanti Asa'ase.
[Japanese] A Japanese god of the earth.
[African] In Yoruba myth, the main creative force, much like the modern concept of God.
[Aztec] An Aztec creator goddess. She is the wife of Ometecuhtli.
[Greek heroic] A queen of the Amazons, by Ares the mother of Penthesilea and Hippolyta.

[Other] Ouroboros ("the tail-devourer") is the symbolization of concepts such as completion, perfection and totality, the endless round of existence, etc. It is usually represented as a worm or serpent with its tail in its mouth.
[Japanese] The Japanese god of the sea.
[Other] A character from Malay folklore who always does the opposite of what is advisable or necessary, and so always fails. The name means "Daddy Stupid".

[Roman] The helmsman of Aeneas, who, while asleep, fell into the sea at the coast of Lucania. He swam to the coast but was killed by the Lucanians. A mountain near that place is named after him (the current Palinuro).
[Greek] Literally, "the all-dewy one". She is a daughter of Cecrops.
[Mesopotamian] The chief minister of the Sumerian gods of heaven, especially of Ea, and messenger of the gods.
[Other] Ancient Finnish household spirits who appear in the shape of a cat, snake, hare, or frog. They enlarge to amount of food and money with what they stole elsewhere.
[Inca] An ancient pre-Inca god of water, rain and storms, as well as a god of creation. He was born as a falcon, but assumed a human form later. He was worshipped in the Central Andes.
[Greek] "Virgin", an epithet of the goddess Athena. The Parthenon is her temple on the Acropolis in Greece.
[Greek] Literally, "alarm". She is one of Graeae, the three old women from Greek myth.
[Other] "Five-fold book". The Greek name for the first five books of the Old Testament (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy), or books of Moses. Called Torah ("the law") by Hebrews.
[Greek heroic] The son of Orestes and Erigone. He is the legendary ancestor of the Penthilids, an ancient royal family on Lesbos.
[Folklore] He is the french form of Santa Claus; the gift bringer to the children of France.
[Greek heroic] In Greek mythology, the robber of Argolis, and a son of Hephaestus. He is called 'the club-bearer' because he murdered his victims with an iron club. The hero Theseus killed him.

[Greek heroic] A Spartan who, during the Messenian wars, fled to Italy. He is regarded as the founder of Tarentum (current Taranto), where he was venerated as a half-god. However, Heracles is also regarded as the founder of the city.

[Greek] A son of Hypnos and one of the Oneiroi, the personifications of the various types of dreams. The various lifeless items one meets in one's dreams are created by him. His name means "apparition".
[Greek heroic] A Greek ship-builder. He constructed the ship with which Paris abducted Helen.
[Greek] The son of Apollo. He was a Thracian singer and musician. His children were Thamyris and Eumolpus.
[Greek] The river that flows with fire which burns and does not consume. It is one of the five principal rivers in the realms of Hades.
[Greek] The offspring of Phorcys and Ceto: the Graeae, the Gorgons, and Echidna.
[Folklore] A fairy or dwarf; anything very small.
[Native American] Among the Karok Indians of northwestern California, the mythic times preceding human times.
[Greek heroic] The son of Pelops, brother of Atreus and Thyestes. According to some he was the father of Agamemnon and Menelaus, whom he had raised by Atreas. Others mention him as a son of Atreus.
[Greek heroic] The son of Asclepius, and, like his brother Machaon, a renowned physician.
[Greek] The son of Asclepius. He and his brother Machaon were renowned as healers.
[Greek heroic] A wise Trojan hero who possessed the gift of prophecy. He was the friend and counselor of Hector.

[Other] A Pontianak is a female Malay vampire. In order to chase its victims, its head detaches from its body with its entrails trailing below. When the head reaches its victim, it sucks his / her blood.
[Greek] One of the giants who fought against the gods. He was killed by Heracles.
[Roman] The Roman goddess of the past.

[Native American] In Crow Indian folklore, and also of the Hidatsa and the Gros Ventre, a terrible old woman. She always keeps a big pot burning, and when she tilts it towards anyone it sucks them in.
[Hindu] In Hindu myth, divine creatures who proceeded from the mind of Brahma, a name applied to some of the deities, but particularly identified with the Rishis.
[Other] The Khmer thunder-god of ancient Cambodia. He rides on a three-headed elephant and casts bolts of lightning. He shows similarities with the Indian god Indra.
[Greek] An appellation of Eros, in the theology of the Orphic-Dionysic Mysteries, as "firstborn" of the primeval egg of Nyx (Night).
[Other] "King of the Wind". The Malay wind-god.
[Other] In Malay mythology, the King of the Sea Serpents, the largest of all the dragons in the ocean. He lives in the Pusat Tasik palace.
[Hindu] The Hindu general of the demon army.

[African] The rain-god of the Bavenda of Transvaal. All the destructive natural phenomena (earthquakes, floods, thunder, drought) as well as plagues are attributed to him. Only the chieftain may address him, with 'grandfather'.
[Hindu] A generalized Hindu term for god or divinity.
[Persian] The ancient Persian god of midday, the protecting deity of the south and of summer.
[Roman] The Roman god of the second ploughing. See also Imporcitor and Vervactor.

[Other] Rimenanwe are the little people of the Marshall Islands. They are rascally little fellows, who mostly steer clear of humans, but like to "borrow" canoes and food and such, as they can get away with it.
[African] The god of the Serer people of Gambia.
[Polynesian] "Water-Food". The Polynesian god of whales who himself appears as a huge whale. He is also the god of comets.
[Other] The Slavic god of war who cult center was on the island of Rugen in the Baltic Sea. His name means "master on Rugen". He is represented with seven heads and holding a sword.
[Islamic] The spirit of God which he breathed into Maryam. Now also a title for the highest mullahs (the ayatollahs in the Iranian Shi'a). Qur'an 4:169, 15:29, 21:91, 32:8, 38:72).
[African] The god of cattle among the Baziba of Africa. He is the son of Wamara.

[Native American] Elected chiefs of the Wabanaki. The sagamores could be deposed if they were behaving badly, but would otherwise serve for life. They generally wielded little power, though the Europeans decided to make them Kings and Queens.
[Hindu] One of the four groups of Vedas, comprising of ceremonies of the Soma.

[Hindu] In Hindu myth, a goddess of the river waters and of fertility and wealth. Sarasvati is the patroness of speech, writing and learning, and of the arts and sciences. She is the consort of Brahma.
[Islamic] "Sword of God". The praise-name of Ali as the destroyer of pagan jinns. Today it is used as a praise name for warriors in the jihad (holy war).
[Greek] The god of the river with the same name, near Troy. He was the father of Teucer and participated in the Trojan War (Iliad XX, 73; XXI, 1).
[Celtic] "Shadowy One". The Irish goddess who instructed Cuchulainn and other warriors in the art of war. She also prophesized Cuchulainn's fame as a hero. Her sister is Aife.
[Greek heroic] The son of Athamas and Themisto, king of Boeotia and father of Atalanta.
[Roman] The personification of security, and its goddess. She was invoked to ensure the stability of the Roman empire.
[Roman] One of the companions of Aeneas. He was the ancestor of the gens Sergia, a renowned Patrician family of Rome, to whom also Catilina belonged (Virgil IV, 288).

[Chinese] A Chinese sea monster that has the head of a tiger and the body of a fish. The body is covered with poisonous spikes. On land it can transform itself into a tiger. A representation of the Shachihoko was used in medieval Japan as a gargoyle.
[African] An angry god of the Yoruba people of Nigeria. He is a son of Yemaja who inflicts humans with the pocks and madness.
[Other] In Malay mythology, a terrible king who commands three regiments: one of flying horses, one of flying lions, and one of flying elephants.
[Japanese] An ancestral spirit in Japanese mythology. Its shape is described as oval or spherical, like a fireball with a bright red color. It is the wandering spirit of a dead person.
[Other] The God of the Sky of the Moksha-Mordvins. He is supreme among the gods, and offerings and prayers must be made to him first, before all other gods.
[Chinese] One of the San-guan. Shui-guan is the Ruler of Water. He helps the believer to overcome obstacles. All three rulers keep a register of the good and evil deed of people.
[Mesopotamian] A divine herald of storm and of bad weather in ancient Mesopotamia.
[Greek] An epithet of Apollo, derived from the Smintha, a city near Troy, or from sminthos; the mouse-exterminator.

[Chinese] The king of the Third Hell of Chinese myth. Here people are punished who were guilty of unfilial behavior, disobedience, disloyalty, and rebellion. He is honored on the eighth day of the Second Moon.
[Greek] The river deity of the river in Thessaly with the same name. He is a son of Gaia and Oceanus.
[Roman] The Roman god who was called upon when people removed thorns from the fields. The name is derived from spina ("spine").
[Roman] A Roman god who took care of the fertilization of farmland (stercus, manure). An alternative name of Saturn or, according to others, Picumnus.
[Native American] Stonecoats [Seneca] and Witiko are North Eastern Woodland cannibals.
[Other] An ancient Slavic fire god, especially of the fire that was used to dry grain. His name survices today in the Rumanian sfarog, "torrid". Svarozic's father is Svarog.
[Polynesian] The Spirit Land in the heart of the earth.
[Other] The chief god of the Niquiran.
[Judaic] A class of angels mentioned in Seder Gan Eden and Sefer Raziel.
[Native American] In Iroquouis myth, the evil twin brother of Ioskeha.
[Other] "The First". In Kiribati myth, a child of Na Atibu and Nei Teuke, the first beings.
[Mayan] The Mayan bird who broke the bones and muscles of the first men who Hurakan destroyed in a flood.

[Egyptian] The personified goddess of moisture in Egyptian mythology. Together with her consort Shu (Air) she was produced by Re from his own body by masturbation. By Shu she became the mother of Seb (Earth) and Nut (Sky).
[Greek heroic] The wife of Agenor, mother of Cadmus, among others.
[Other] The Estonian god who forged the sun and placed her in the heavens.
[Aztec] The Aztec mother of the gods.
[Judaic] The first four books of the Bible. It is composed of the Books of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers.
[Greek heroic] A queen of the Amazons who went with 300 women to meat Alexander the Great, in the hope of raising a race of Alexanders.
[Greek heroic] The son of Polynices, one of the Epigonoi. He marched with the Greeks against Troy, but was killed by Telephus in Mysia, where he was later venerated as a hero.
[Other] The god of thunder of the Chibcha of Colombia.

[Haitian] The trickster in the folklore of the Negroes of Haiti (as well as of other parts of the Creole-speaking New World -- Martinique, Guadeloupe, Lesser Antilles). In Haiti, and elsewhere, his foil is the lumbering Uncle Bouki.
[Chinese] The conventional expression to designate the universe. It means literally "Heaven and Earth".
[Chinese] The Chinese goddess of lightning whose name means "Mother of Lightning".

[Native American] The younger brother of Kwatyat who allow themselves to be swallowed by a monster in order to save their mother who had been ingested earlier. Once inside they cut through the monster's stomach thus allowing for their escape.
[Folklore] A half-man half-horse creature from Philippine folklore. It lives in secluded areas in swamps. It is said that the knees of the tikbalang rise above its head, hiding its face.
[Polynesian] A Polynesian head-ache demon, one of the two Ponaturi that managed to escape Urutonga's revenge for the death of her husband.
[Native American] Tornarsuk is the chief god of the Eskimos. He resides in the underworl and is the leader of the tornat, Eskimo guardian deities.
[Native American] A very important Eskimo god, the Good Being.
[Hindu] The triad of the great Hindu gods which proceeded from the world-egg deposited by the supreme First Cause: Brahma, the Creator; Vishnu, the Preserver; and Shiva, the Destroyer.
[Basque] In Basque mythology, they are the spirits of the hurricanes that come from the sea.
[Greek heroic] The son of the Boeotian king Erginus, and brother of Agamedes (q.v.).
[Native American] The Navaho sun deity. Each day he crosses the heavens with the sun on his back. To rest, he hangs the sun on a peg on the west wall in his house.
[Native American] The Cherokee god of hunting.
[Polynesian] The Polynesian South Wind. It was the first of the winds to be brought under control by Maui. Hakona Tipu is also a name for the South Wind.
[Etruscan] An Etruscan demoness of the underworld. It is a horrible, winged creature with snake-hair and the beak of a bird.
[Other] The Creator-god of Tarascan people of Central America
[Other] The Wagawaga (New Guinea) god who lives with his wife and children in Hiyoyoa, the land of the dead. He directs the spirits of the dead, telling them where to make their gardens.

[Folklore] In medieval legend, a demon who collects all the words skipped over or mutilated by priests in the celebration of the Mass. These he deposits in that pit which is said to be paved with 'good intentions' never brought to effect.
[Basque] Red calf genie that, according to Basque mythology, lives in caves and gorges.
[Judaic] An angel mentioned in Sefer Yetzirah and Zohar. He is the good angel who escorts the indidivual home on the eve of Sabbath.
[Judaic] An angel of the Countenance mentioned in Maasah Merkavah.
[Mayan] "House of the Water". Created as a wife for the four men made from maize paste. She became the wife of Mahucutah.
[Mesopotamian] A king of Shurrupak (modern Fara, north-west of Uruk) and father of Utnapishtim. The only king of Kish named in the pre-diluvian King-List, apart from Utnapishtim.
[Other] A Hittite mountain god who carried the edge of the sky, where the sun sets, on his shoulders.
[Inca] In Inca mythology, Uca Pacha ("the lower world") is the underworld which lies in the center of the earth. It is a cold and dark place, where the souls of the damned are eternally hungry.
[Aztec] The Aztec god of sex and irresponsible gaiety. His name means "Old, Old Coyote".
[Other] The demon of oil who is always burning. He is charged with the task of replenishing the cauldrons in hell.
[Native American] A land creature often depicted as dragon-like and was the source of mysterious deaths and inexplicable disappearances.
[African] The greator god of the Basari of Togo (west Africa).
[Hindu] A series of Hindu sacred texts, philosophical commentaries to the Vedas.
[Polynesian] According to Samoan myth, the first woman on the island of Upolu.
[Inca] The Inca god of underground treasures.
[Mesopotamian] The two-faced attendant of the Babylonian god Ea.

[Other] The highest of the four categories of gods in Jainism (old-Indian Work of Salvation), next to the Vyantara, the Jyotisha, and the Bhavanavasi. The Vimanika live in mobile palaces in the heavens.
[Other] The third Dhyani-Buddha of Nepal to whom the final part of the night is dedicated. His color is white and his attributes are a bolt of lightning (vajra) and a clock.
[Hindu] In Hinduism, one of the Rishis and also one of the Prajapatis. He was the owner of Nandi, the white bull of Shiva.
[Native American] The name for "Greasy Mouth" an eccentric and erratic culture hero and might be derived from the Algonquin Wesucechak.
[Roman] The Roman god of the first ploughing. See also Imporcitor and Redarator.
[Roman] An ancient Roman goddess of victory. She had a temple located at the base of the Velia.
[Hindu] In Hindu myth, a monster created by Shiva in his quarrel with Daksha.
[Inca] The supreme Inca god, synthesis of sun-god and storm-god.
[Hindu] An Indian primeval being, created by Brahma.
[Roman] The Roman goddess to whom spouses made offering when they had domestic problems.
[Roman] The Roman god of courage and military prowess.
[Hindu] The Hindu divine artificer, craftsman and smith.
[Other] In Finno-Ugric and Magyar mythology, an extremely unlikeable and ugly water god. He lived in rivers and lakes and regularly demanded human sacrifices.
[Other] The Slavic werewolf. The name comes from vlko, "wolf".
[Roman] A river deity associated with the river Volturnus in Campania (Italy), but it could also be an ancient name for the Tiber. The Volturnalia was observed on August 27.
[Norse] In Norse mythology, Vor was the goddess of marriage and contracts from whom nothing could be hidden because she was so wise. She was the goddess of faithfulness between man and woman.
[Folklore] A vampire-like creature from Greek folklore. It is an animated corpse that can leave its grave on any day except Saturday. It can be killed by fire or by a stroke of lightning.
[Roman] The Roman god of the East Wind, equal to the Greek Eurus.
[Polynesian] "Long Branch". The Polynesian god of comets.
[Polynesian] A Polynesian hero-god, son of Tawhaiki.
[Native American] Dust devil, small whirlwind, youngest brother to the Four winds.

[Native American] The Sioux prophet who initiated the Dream Dance in 1876 which would protect and restore Native Americans to a time before white intervention. Practiced by the Ojibwa, Potawatomi, Fox, and Kickapoo tribes.
[Native American] The creator and supreme being of the Yaghan Indians. He is the master of life and death, and he also rules over the animal kingdom. His name means "ancient".

[Chinese] The Chinese deity who guards the back door of domestic dwellings and public buildings. A former minister of emperor Tang Tai-zong, Wei Cheng is far less popular as a guardian of doorways then the Men-shen.
[Chinese] The protector of the teaching. Often found in the company of Guan-yin.
[Other] The supreme god of the Luo of Kenya. He controls life and death, and he strikes down wrongdoers with thunderbolts.
[Native American] A wizard or a male evil doer.
[Other] In Thai mythology, the architect of the gods. The name is a combination of Vishnu and Kama.

[Aboriginal] The Aboriginal giant snake which is associated with the rainbow and worshipped a creator of life. The snake emerged from a lake in the Murschison Mountains where the life-bringing rains are collected.
[Other] Wurukatte is the proto-Hattic god of war. Called 'the king of the realm' he was worshipped in Asia Minor. To the Hittites he is Zababa, the war-god they adopted from the Akkadians.

[Other] The proto-Hattic sun goddess of Asia Minor. Wurusemu also appears as an earth goddess and is then the wife of the weather god Taru and mother of Telipinu, a vegetation god. Wurusemu shows many similarities with the Hittite goddess Arinna.
[Hindu] One of the four groups of Vedas, consisting of sacrificial texts.
[Other] The Ugaritic god of the wathers. He is the arch-enemy of Baal.
[Other] According to the Lapps of Northern Scandinavia, Yambe-akka is the queen of the underworld.
[Native American] The great medicine man of the Zuni. He is associated with civilization, agriculture, animal husbandry, social life, healing and knowledge.

[Chinese] The Chinese Goat God. Peasants in the mountainous regions make sacrifices to Yang Jing for protection against wild animals. He is depicted with a goat's head worn like a bonnet and a goatskin.
[Korean] The eldest of three demi-god brothers, appearing in the Samseong myth.

[Chinese] Literally "feather men". In ancient times, the feather men were flying immortals (see Xian), whose bodies were covered with a coat of feathers. Now it is an alternative designation for a Taoist priest.

[Japanese] The Lady of the Snow, the Snow Queen or Winter Ghost in Japanese mythology. Sometimes she appears as an earthly woman, marries and has children, but sometimes she will disappear in a white mist.
[Judaic] A race of giants who once lived in Ammon (Deuteronomy 2:20-1)
[Islamic] One of the fountains in paradise. Also ginger, a special beverage for the blessed (Qur'an 76:17).
[Persian] Zarich is one of the female members of the Daevas and the personification of ageing. Her eternal opponent is Ameretat.

[Other] A Lithuanian earth and fertility god, protector of cattle and homestead. Zemepates is also called Dimstipatis, from dimstis, home, and patis, father. He is supposed to be a brother of the earth goddess Zemyna. His Latvian equivalent is Majas gars.
[Judaic] One of the minor prophets in the Bible. The Book of Zephaniah, which is a vivid prediction of the Day of Judgment, was probably composed in the seventh century BCE.
[Basque] Adult reddish bull genie that, according to Basque mythology, lives in subterranean dwellings and guards them.
[Chinese] The Chinese Taoist god of the afterlife, and a god of exorcism. His Japanese equivalent is Shoki.
[Other] A spirit of the Songhai, Africa. This blind spirit is the Master of Fish.
[Other] The Slavonic virgin goddess of war. She is closely associated with Perun or his various incarnations.

[Judaic] Rabbah ben Abuha. Talmudic Sage. He ascended to the Garden of Eden while still alive. As a result, when he returned to earth all of his clothing bore the fragrance of Eden, a scent so enchanting he made a fortune selling his garments (B.M. 112).
The lowest level of power production needs during a season or year.

A biodegradable transportation fuel for use in diesel engines that is produced through the transesterfication of organically- derived oils or fats. It may be used either as a replacement for or as a component of diesel fuel.
A provision included in some power sale contracts that lets the supplier stop delivery when the power is needed to meet certain other obligations.
A mass of coal, occurring naturally at a particular location, that can be commercially mined.
Unwanted natural gas that is disposed of by burning as it is released from an oil field.
A device used to collect solar energy. It is a piece of metal painted black on the side facing the sun, to absorb the sun's heat.
A unit of illuminance on a surface that is one foot from a uniform point source of light of one candle and is equal to one lumen per square foot.
The area of a surface including areas not belonging to that surface (such as windows and doors in a wall).

An increase in the amount of heat contained in a space, resulting from direct solar radiation, heat flow through walls, windows, and other building surfaces, and the heat given off by people, lights, equipment, and other sources.
A decrease in the amount of heat contained in a space, resulting from heat flow through walls, windows, roof and other building surfaces and from exfiltration of warm air.
The difference between scheduled and actual power flows on electric transmission lines.

A complete lighting unit consisting of a lamp or lamps together with the parts designed to distribute the light, to position and protect the lamps and to connect the lamps to the power supply. California Code of Regulations, Section 2- 1602(h)].
A common term for gas that bubbles to the surface of the water in a marsh or swamp. It is colorless, odorless and can be explosive.
The highest electrical demand within a particular period of time. Daily electric peaks on weekdays occur in late afternoon and early evening. Annual peaks occur on hot summer days.
Two or more interconnected utilities that plan and operate to supply electricity in the most reliable, economical way to meet their combined load.
The heating of oil shale to get the oil out from it.
Scheduled operating level for each generating unit or other resource scheduled to run in the Hour-ahead Schedule.

Vertical shading elements mounted on either side of a glazed opening that blocks direct solar radiation from the lower, lateral portions of the sun's path. SITE -- any location on which a facility is constructed or is proposed to be constructed.

(Electric Utility) - The basis for settling economy-energy transactions between utilities. The added costs of the supplier are subtracted from the avoided costs of the buyer, and the difference is evenly divided.
A bid into the PX indicating a price at which a seller is prepared to sell energy or ancillary services.
Sedimentary rocks containing heavy oil that cannot be extracted by conventional petroleum recovery methods.

(Variable Air Volume System) - A mechanical HVAC system capable of serving multiple zones which controls the temperature maintained in a zone by controlling the amount of heated or cooled air supplied to the zone.

Two separate samples with separate containers taken at the same time and at the same place.
a relatively homogeneous ecological area defined by similarity of climate, landform, soil, potential natural vegetation, hydrology, or other ecologically relevant variables (see also bioregions).
Negatively charged building blocks of an atom that circle around the nucleus.
To purify, separate, or remove by washing, decanting, and settling.

A predetermined plan of action to be taken to reduce the potential for property damage and loss of lives in a downstream area affected by a dam break or excessive spillway discharges.
Devices used to hold the rotor and stator of a motor in position.
Located or occurring within a glacier.
A plant that grows on another plant but is not a parasite and produces its own food by photosynthesis, as certain orchids, mosses, and lichens; an air plant.
A Hydrothermal mineral deposit formed within approximately one kilometer (0.6 mile) of the earth's surface and in the temperature range of 50°C (122°F) to 200°C (392°F).
Capable of living in a wide range of water depths. Use of an aquatic organism.
Reservoirs and lakes which are rich in nutrients and very productive in terms of aquatic animal and plant life.

Sediments deposited from an aqueous (water) solution as a result of extensive or local evaporation of a solvent, such as salts in the Great Salt Lake in the western United States.
(Botanical) Remaining verdant, as coniferous trees and many tropical plants. Contrasted with Deciduous whose leaves, fruit, or petals fall at the end of the growing period.

A plant community where Evergreen trees or shrubs represent more than 50 percent of the total areal coverage of trees and shrubs. The canopy is never without foliage; however, individual trees or shrubs may shed their leaves.
(Water Quality) The violation of the pollutant levels permitted by environmental protection standards.
A water impoundment made by constructing a dam or embankment or by excavating a pit or "dug out".
(Water Quality) Water input into a desalting or water treatment plant.

Of particles that are sufficiently small to allow their passage through filters capable of retaining most particles. For example, a filterable virus is one that will pass through a filter that will normally retain bacteria.

The maximum annual supply of a given water development that is expected to be available on demand, with the understanding that lower yields will occur in accordance with a predetermined schedule or probability. Sometimes referred to as Dependable Yield.
The highest level to which the fresh snow on a glacier's surface retreats during the melting season; the line separating the accumulation area from the ablation area.
the sudden death of fish due to the introduction of pollutants or the reduction of the dissolved oxygen concentration in a water body.
Of or on a level or slow-moving watercourse.
The maximum instantaneous discharge of a flood at a given location. It usually occurs at or near the time of the flood crest, i.e., the maximum stage or elevation reached by the flood flow.
A distinct rise in stage, culminating in a crest and followed by recession to lower stages.

The land bordering a stream which is subject to floods of about equal frequency; for example, a strip of the floodplain subject to flooding more often than once, but not as frequently as twice in a century (100-Year Flood).
The water of a flood. Often used in the plural (Floodwaters).
A device which allows for measurement of stream flow by measuring velocity in a given cross-sectional area.
A graphical representation of flow lines and Equipotential Lines for two-dimensional, steady-state ground-water flow.
An incinerator that uses a bed of hot sand or other granular material to transfer heat directly to waste. Used mainly for destroying municipal sludge.
The addition of a chemical to increase the concentration of fluoride ions in drinking water to reduce the incidence of tooth decay.
An abnormal condition caused by excessive intake of Fluorine, as from fluoridated drinking water, characterized chiefly by mottling of the teeth.
A pump with a solid piston and valves used to raise a liquid or expel it under pressure.
the combination of active and inactive (inert) ingredients which make up a pesticide.
(Hydraulics) Flow through or over a structure not affected by submergence or backwater.
The depth to which frost penetrates the earth.
Gallons per day per foot. The unit of measure to describe transmissivity of an aquifer.
A system where two (2) or more water wells are coupled together with a common header or manifold.
(Irrigation) Portable pipe with small gates installed along one side for distributing water to corrugations or furrows.
The art or science of cultivating the earth; husbandry.

A periodic thermal spring that results from the expansive force of super heated steam. Also, a special type of thermal spring which intermittently ejects a column of water and steam into the air with considerable force.
An early forest successional stage where grasses and forbs are the dominant vegetation.

Waste water from a household or small commercial establishment which specifically excludes water from a toilet, kitchen sink, dishwasher, or water used for washing diapers. More commonly spelled Greywater.
wastewater other than sewage, such as sink or washing machine drainage.
domestic wastewater that does not contain human wastes such as tub, shower, or washing machine water.
The boundary between surface fresh water and underlying saltwater in a stratified coastal environment. A location where there is a marked change in salinity.
type of crusher or shredder used to break up waste materials into smaller pieces.

A steep slope or precipice rising at the head of a valley or glacial Cirque.
A mark indicating the highest level reached by a body of water.
Horsepower calculated from electric units whereby 746 watts of electrical energy is equivalent to one horsepower.
A spring that brings hot water to the surface. A thermal spring. Water temperature usually 15F (8C) or more above the mean air temperature.
(Botany) A water-excreting microscopic epidermal structure in many plants.

A graphic representation of the variation in stream qualities, such as discharge, stage, or temperature. These data are plotted against time on the graph. This is also done for ground water and surface water levels.
Having a strong affinity for water.
(1) An abnormal fear of water. (2) Rabies.
An electrical instrument for detecting or monitoring sound transmitted through water.
A map or graph displaying temporal or areal distribution of precipitation.
Plants extremely sensitive to dry air, growing only in habitats where relative humidity is always high. Also see Hydrophyte.
A wedge-shaped structure for protecting a bridge pier from floating ice.
Of or relating to a strain of genetically altered bacteria that are applied to crop plants to inhibit the formation of frost.
A thin ice crystal floating high in the atmosphere in certain conditions of clear, cold weather.
The temperature, equal to 1.0°C (33.8°F), at which pure water and ice are in equilibrium in a mixture at 1 atmosphere of pressure.
A very large Ice Cap, also called continental glacier, as that of the antarctic continent.
A storm in which snow or rain freezes on contact, forming a coat of ice on the surfaces it touches.
Curves developed by the Department of Transportation to determine rainfall Intensity-Duration Frequency.

(Geology) Of or relating to one of the glacial stages of the Pleistocene epoch which occurred in North America, which consisted of the Nebraskan (first stage), Kansan (second stage), Illinoian (third stage), and Wisconsin (fourth stage).
Particles or other objects that cause water to be unclear.
(Water Quality) Nonpathogenic bacteria whose presence in water indicate the possibility of pathogenic species in the water.
(New England) A tract of low-lying land, especially along a river.
Gathering data needed for analyses and evaluation of the status or condition of a specific universe or area of concern.
A device that measures the intensity of ionizing radiation.
Indicating equal rainfall, generally expressed as lines of equal rainfall.
Having, or denoting, equal pressure; Isobaric.
In Limnology, a state in which a lake is at the same temperature throughout and is well-mixed. Periods of isothermy occur in Spring and Autumn in Dimictic Lakes.
A fine, powdered diatomaceous earth used in industry as a filler, a filtering agent, and absorbent, a clarifier, and an insulator. More commonly referred to as Diatomite.
The rate of change of temperature with height in the free atmosphere.
(Geology) A solidified mass of rock formed when a stream of viscous, molten lave from a volcano or fissure has cooled and congealed.
(Nautical) A line marked at intervals of fathoms and weighted at one end, used to determine the depth of water. Also referred to as a Sounding Line.
The left-hand bank of a stream viewed when the observer faces downstream.
A violent storm or a series of storms of rain and wind believed to take place during the equinoxes.
Lying close to water or ground level as low-lying coastal areas.
The lowest level attained by a varying water surface level.
A member of the macroscopic plant life, especially of a body of water.
municipal waste combustion technology in which solid waste is burned in a controlled system without prior sorting or processing.
The average depth of water in a stream channel or conduit. It is equal to the cross-sectional area divided by the surface width.
A condition of permanent stratification of water masses in lakes.
Term to characterize waters with salinity of 5 to 18 0/00 (parts per thousand), due to ocean-derived salts.

A plant that grows under medium or usual conditions of atmospheric moisture supply, as distinguished from one which grows under dry or desert conditions (Xerophyte) or very wet conditions (Hydrophyte).
Term to characterize waters with salinity of 5 to 18 0/00 (parts per thousand), due to land-derived salts.
The division of the Atmosphere above the Stratosphere. The mesosphere begins about 50 kilometers (31 miles) in altitude and extends to about 80 kilometers (50 miles).
Conversion of food, for instance soluble organic matter, to cellular matter and gaseous by-products through a biological process.
The plants, animals, and microorganisms that can only be seen with the aid of a microscope.
One one-thousandth of a Milligram per Liter (mg/l). This measure is equivalent to Parts Per Billion (PPB).
A unit of length equivalent to a micro-meter (µm), or one-millionth of a meter (10-6 meter). Micro-meter is the preferred term.

A smaller permanent pool used in a stormwater pond due to extenuating circumstances, i.e., concern over the thermal impacts of larger ponds, impacts on existing marshes, or lack of topographic relief.
The rapid stream of water flowing in a Millrace.
A drawing to scale which depicts an applicant's or permittee's property boundaries and which identifies approximate time frames by month and year for areas to be mined or dewatered.
Water-deposited accumulation of sandy, silty, or clayey material recently eroded in mining operations.
Term to characterize water with salinity of 0.5 to 30 0/00 (parts per thousand), due to ocean salts. The term is roughly equivalent to the term brackish.
Term to characterize water with salinity of 0.5 to 30 0/00 (parts per thousand), due to land-derived salts.
the smallest portions of a substance having the properties of the substance.
A stream bed made up of materials readily transportable by the streamflow.
(Water Quality) Accretions of siliceous incrustations on the exterior of sand grains in a rapid sand filter; typically removed by backwashing. Such deposits interfere with effective filtration.

A tide that occurs when the difference between high and low tide is least; the lowest level of high tide. Neap tide comes twice a month, in the first and third quarters of the moon. Contrast with Spring Tide.

(Geology) Of or relating to one of the glacial stages of the Pleistocene epoch which occurred in North America, which consisted of the Nebraskan (first stage), Kansan (second stage), Illinoian (third stage), and Wisconsin (fourth stage).
Something which does not allow water to pass through it. More specifically, a material with no void spaces.
Any process by which the phase change of a substance to a more condensed state (condensation, sublimation, freezing) is initiated at certain loci, nuclei, within the less condensed state.
(Sports) Existing or taking place on snow that has not been compacted into tracks.
A thin, glistening layer of oil on the surface of water.
Cropland that is no longer used to produce an agricultural crop and that has been allowed to revert to natural plant cover.
Forests that either have never been cut or have not been cut for many decades. Forests characterized by a large percentage of mature trees.
n organism that obtains nutrients through the active uptake of so
A Flume (or bridge with sideboards) for passing flood water across an irrigation ditch or canal.
(Botany) The uppermost, or tree, part of a forest, formed by tree crowns; canopy.
Application of ozone to water for disinfection or for taste and odor control. The ozonator is the device that does this.
Water, at a desirable temperature, that is free from objectionable tastes, odors, colors, and turbidity.
Pertaining to a Marsh or Wetlands; wet or marsh habitats.
The maximum instantaneous discharge of a stream or river at a given location. It usually occurs at or near the time of maximum stage.
