The scientific study of soils, their origins, characteristics, and uses.
A District computer program, used by the clerical staff to requisition office supplies.
A unit of measure for levels of radon gas; becquerels per cubic meter is metric equivalent.
Synonymous with Hydraulic Head, which is now commonly used.
(Physics) The measurement of the compressibility of liquids.
A diagram or photo showing a facility as it would appear when looking down on top of it.

A temporary lake formed in a Playa. A shallow, intermittent lake in an arid region, occupying a playa in the wet season but drying up in the summer; an ephemeral lake that upon evaporation leaves or forms a playa.
Term to characterize water with salinity of 18 to 30 0/00 (parts per thousand), due to ocean salts.
Term to characterize water with salinity of 18 to 30 0/00 (parts per thousand), due to land-derived salts.
A mass of filamentous algae forming a green scum on the surface of ponds and other such bodies of water.
That portion of rock or soil not occupied by solid mineral matter and which may be occupied by ground water.
An apparatus for measuring the rate of transpiration in a plant by determining the amount of water absorbed.
The lowest temperature at which a liquid will pour under given conditions.

An EPA initiative to give states and the regulated community the flexibility to develop comprehensive strategies as alternatives to multiple current regulatory requirements in order to exceed compliance and increase overall environmental benefits.
(Geology) A type of Hydrothermal alteration characterized by the formation of calcite, chlorite, epidote, serpentine, quartz, pyrite, and iron oxides.

small single-cell microbes; frequently observed as actively moving organisms when impure water is viewed under a microscope; cause a number of widespread human illnesses, such as malaria, and thus can present a threat to public health.
The distance between the ground water table and the overlying land surface.
(1) The area indicated on a weather map over which rain fell within a certain period of time. (2) The area over which rain is falling. (3) The most rainy portion of a cyclonic storm.
The portion of rainfall which reaches a stream channel or concentration point as direct surface flow.
The material settled out during the primary clarification of sewage.
In water pollution, chemicals that are soluble in water at a concentration equal to or greater than one milligram per liter (mg/l).
To cause (something Dehydrated) to take up fluid.
A recession of the sea or other water body leaving land uncovered. Also, the land so left uncovered. Also see Dereliction.
The surface area of a reservoir when filled to controlled retention water level.
Movement of an organism in response to a current of water or air.
The right-hand side of a stream, river, or channel when facing in the direction of the flow.
Barren alluvial land, usually coarse-textured, exposed along streams at low water, and subject to shifting during normal high water.
Finely ground rock particles produced by glacial abrasion. Also referred to as Glacier Meal.
(Botany) A thin, hairlike outgrowth of an epidermal cell of a plant root that absorbs water and minerals from the surrounding soil.
The part of the soil that is, or can be, penetrated by plant roots (Soil Conservation Society of America, 1982).
An incinerator with a rotating combustion chamber that keeps waste moving, thereby allowing it to vaporize for easier burning.
The process whereby soluble salts accumulate in the soil.
A salt-encrusted flat area resulting from evaporation of a former body of water.
A landlocked body of water that has become salty through evaporation.
A body of water too salty for most freshwater uses.
(Irrigation) A device, often a simple enlargement in a ditch or conduit, for arresting the heavier particles of sand and silt carried by the water.

(1) A Finnish steam bath in which the steam is produced by pouring water over heated rocks; a bathhouse or room for taking such a steam bath. (2) A dry heat bath; a room or an enclosure for taking a dry heat bath.

The primary toxin produced by dinoflagellate protozoans during blooms known as Red Tides in marine waters. The genus or protozoan involved in the generation of the red color in the water is Ganyaulax. Also see Paralytic Shellfish Poisoning.
A hydrologic computation method for estimation of runoff from rainfall information that has been developed by the United States Department of Agriculture's Soil Conservation Service (SCS).
Soil, sand, and minerals washed from land into water, usually after rain.
(Geology) Worn away nearly to the base level, as at the end of an erosion cycle.
Water, usually storm runoff, flowing in a thin layer over the ground surface (Soil Conservation Society of America, 1982).
The flow of water, initiated from a rainfall event, where the soil surface became saturated and the accumulated water, in puddles, begins to flow in rather thin layers across the land surface.
An extension of glacial ice into coastal waters that is in contact with the bottom near the shore but not toward the outer edge of the shelf.
One of several families of often long-legged wading birds that inhabit the seacoast and shallow fresh-water bodies including sandpipers, stilts, killdeer, avocets, plovers and others.
Land situated on the edge of a body of water.
A fixture for directing the spray of water in a bathroom shower.
f: Any drainage or flood discharge that is released from a specified area.

Soil and rock material that is being or has been moved down a slope predominantly by the action of gravity assisted by running water that is not concentrated into channels. The term applies to the process as well as the materials.

A measure of the time biological solids are retained in a basin calculated by dividing the mass of volatile solids in the basin by the total mass of volatile solids wasted during a given time period. Expressed in units of time.
The vertical distance between the surface of a snow layer and the ground beneath.

A fence of slat and wire or other material used in winter to intercept drifting snow, thus protecting roads, railways, and other areas from snowdrifts. Also, fences used to impound snow where melting in place will add to the soil moisture content.
An area, usually at high elevation or in polar latitudes, where snow accumulates and remains on the ground throughout the entire year.
A graduated fixed pole or staff used to measure snow depth.
A planting of shrubs or other plants to intercept drifting snow. Also referred to as Snowbreak and Snow Catch.
A sample of soil taken by forcing a cylindrical device into the ground perpendicular to the horizontal. The resulting sample contains a circular section of each layer of sediment.
The slow mass movement of soil materials down slopes primarily under the influence of gravity, but facilitated by saturation with water and/or by alternating freezing and thawing.
landfill liner composed of compacted soil or synthetic material designed to assist in containment of leachate.
Water present in the soil pores. Also referred to as Soil Moisture which includes Water Vapor.
A pool of salt water heated by the sun and used either as a direct source of heat or to provide power for an electric generator.
To make (substances such as fats and lipids) soluble in water by the action of a detergent or similar agent.
A spacecraft's soft landing on the water, thereby permitting recovery of personnel and critical components.
A graduated scale used to indicate the height of the water surface in a stream channel, reservoir, lake, or other water body.
r: An entity that holds a special interest in an issue or program -- such as the storm water program -- since it is or may be affected by it.
A steam that is so hot that no water droplets are present in it.
An impoundment, the principal purpose of which is to supply water to livestock. May include reservoirs, pits, and tanks.
n: A slotted opening leading to an underground pipe or an open ditch for carrying surface runoff.
Infiltration plus depression storage; may also include interception loss.
The channel through which a natural stream of water runs or used to run, as a dry streambed.
(Water Quality) A means of predicting the effects upon dissolved oxygen levels of organic loading to a stream based on the deaeration and reaeration rates, and resulting in an Oxygen Sag Curve.
an open mineral mine (Examples: coal, copper, zinc, etc.) where the topsoil and overburden is removed to expose and extract the mineral.
(1) A portion of a subregion or basin drained by a single stream or group of minor streams. (2) The smallest unit into which the land surface is subdivided for hydrologic study purposes.
Existing, formed, or taking place in or under water.
Formed or deposited beneath a glacier.
A small meander contained within the banks of a main channel, associated with relatively low discharges.
A pump designed and so placed in a Sump to remove the water or other liquids collected there.
To cool a liquid below a transition temperature without the transition occurring, especially to cool below the freezing point of water without solidification into ice.
common name for the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act (CERCLA) designed to clean up abandoned or inactive hazardous waste dump sites.
An additional monetary charge levied by a utility over and above the fixed and variable charge portions of the rate structure.
A Translatory Wave in an open channel resulting from a sudden change in flow of water, such as that caused by opening or closing a gate.
The study of different natural communities or Ecosystems.
Water which runs off on the land surface after application from an irrigation system. It is sometimes reused through collection in ponds.
Water withdrawn directly from a tap or faucet.
a box, usually made of glass, that is used for keeping and observing small animals or plants.
An extensive flat tract of land alternatively covered and uncovered by the tide, and comprising mostly unconsolidated mud and sand. Also referred to as Tide Flat.
A swinging gate on the outside of a drainage conduit from a diked field that excludes water at high tide and permits drainage at low tide.
Habitat in the rocky intertidal zone that retains some water at low tide.
A section of the 1990 amendments to the federal Clean Air Act that addresses the control of toxic air emissions. For more information, click here.
a device that is placed inside the tank portion of a toilet to reduce the amount of water the tank will hold by partitioning off part of the tank.
The elevation of the uppermost surface of a dam excluding any parapet wall, railings, etc.
Energy contained by fluid because of its pressure, velocity, and elevation, usually expressed in feet of fluid (foot-pounds per pound).
A pathological condition in a person or animal caused by the presence of a toxic substance in the body.
Refers to the movement of water from one reservoir or storage facility to another.
A screen located at an intake fixture of a dam spillway or other such conduit to prevent the ingress of debris.
Designed to operate on land, water, or in air.
Total Solids. The weight of all present solids per unit volume of water. It is usually determined by evaporation. The total weight concerns both dissolved and suspended organic and inorganic matter.
A current in which a limited volume of turbid or muddy water moves relative to surrounding water because of its greater density.
A drain that carries away water from prepared beds or agricultural fields to which water or wastewater has been applied.
Plants growing beneath the canopy of other plants. Usually refers to grasses, forbs, and low shrubs under a tree or shrub overstory.
A net rainfall one-inch deep which occurs over all parts of a drainage area at a uniform rate during a specified unit period of time.
an area that is highly populated, such as a city or town.
The gaseous flow of water vapor in soils from a moist or warm zone of higher potential to a drier or colder zone of lower potential.

(Biology) The separation or division of a group of organisms by a geographic barrier, such as a mountain or a body of water, resulting in differentiation of the original group into new varieties or species.
Ratio of volume of intergranular voids to volume of solid material in a sediment or sedimentary rock.
In a stream system, the relatively fine material in near-permanent suspension which is transported entirely through the system without deposition.
Water used as the solvent for coatings such a paint.
The rate of flow of water measured in volume and time (e.g., cubic feet per second, or cfs).
A traverse cleft in a mountain ridge through which a stream flows; the gap cut through a resistant ridge by a superimposed or Antecedent Stream.
A dessert made of finely crushed ice that has been sweetened and flavored.
A law that has been instigated to control the right to the use of water. See (Prior) Appropriation Doctrine and Riparian Doctrine.
A document of issues, policies, strategies and action plans intended to effectively and economically execute a Water Planning process. Also see Water Policy.
Land rendered unproductive because of excessive irrigation.
The 12-month period, October 1 through September 30. The water year is designated by the calendar year in which it ends. Therefore, the 1996 water year ends on September 30, 1996.

The process of waterflooding an oil well; to pump water into the ground around an oil well nearing depletion in order to loosen and force out additional oil.
(1) Land abutting a body of water. (2) The part of a town or city that abuts water, especially a district of wharves where ships dock.
(1) Lacking water; dry. (2) Not requiring water, as a cooling system.
A strip of metal, rubber, or other material used to prevent leakage through joints between adjacent sections of concrete.

(Engineering) Openings left in retaining walls, aprons, linings, or foundations to permit drainage and reduce pressure. A hole (as in a wall or foundation) that is designed to drain off accumulated water. Also referred to as Weeper.
(Irrigation) The wide, basinlike approach to the upstream side of a weir, being constructed so as to reduce to a minimum the effect of the momentum of the approaching water on the flow over the weir.
The opening in a weir for the passage of water.
A record that is kept during well drilling of the various formations and rock materials and the depths at which they are encountered. Synonymous with Water Well Report.
An arrangement or device approved by the District that prevents contaminants from entering the well at the upper terminus.
The volume of water discharged from a well in gallons per minute or cubic meters per day.

Multiple wells under common ownership or control, which may or may not be located on contiguous land parcels, intended to supply a common service area. Term usually associated with public water supply.
Grassland with waterlogged soil near the surface but without standing water for most of the year.
A person who lives in proximity to Wetlands and whose culture is linked to them.

A systematic arrangement of words and/or numbers used for expressing and recording the velocity or force of the wind. The U.S. Weather Bureau scale uses a graduation of 13 scales (0-12) to represent different wind conditions. Also see Beaufort's Scale.
The side walls of a structure used to prevent sloughing of banks or channels and to direct and confine overfall.
Any biological substance, displaced from its normal habitat; a chemical foreign to a biological system.

Any plant growing in a habitat in which an appreciable portion of the rooting medium dries to the wilting coefficient at frequent intervals. A drought resistant plant; a plant which grows in arid areas.

Flood lantern which uses a parabolic reflector and a low voltage high intensity lamp to produce an intense near-parallel beam. Also known as a Beam Projector.

Lamps arranged around the stage directed into the auditorium , originally to prevent spectators seeing the stage during scene changes when the house tabs were not lowered. Now used for effect in rock concerts etc.
The process of arranging moves to be made by the actors during the play, recorded by stage management in the prompt script.
Metal bin or box covered with fine mesh in which Theatrical Maroons can be safely detonated.
Two-fold piece of scenery. Book flats are free-standing when angled open, allowing quick setting and compact storage. Booking describes the action of opening or closing a book flat.
US term for a front of house vertical lighting position (predominantly sidelight).
A U-shaped clip and saddle used for terminating wire rope. Also known as a Bulldog, Dog Grip or Wire Rope Clip.
Lockable (and sometimes releasable) plastic strap used to tie a bundle of cables together, amongst many other things.
Circular slide magazine; also refers to a 35mm slide projector using this type of magazine (Kodak trade name). See Projection.
Auditorium working lights. Used for cleaning and setting up the auditorium before the house lights (usually more atmospheric) are switched on.
Distortion in a sound signal caused by an amplifier or mixer being unable to handle the level of signal being fed to it.
The use of colour filters to compensate for the different colour temperatures of different light sources. Important in lighting for TV and film.
Bringing another lighting state up to completely replace the current lighting state. Also applies to sound effects / music. Sometimes abbreviated to Xfade or XF.
Cutting out action and dialogue between cues during a technical rehearsal, to save time.

A floodlight, usually with an asymmetrical reflector, designed to light a cyc or backcloth from the top or bottom. In the US, a flood at the top of the cyc is a CYC OVER, and a flood at the bottom is a CYC UNDER.
To fly an item without a counterweight.
A room with very thick sound absorbers, causing a very dull sound with no reverberation.
Electrical or electronic device which controls the amount of electricity passed to a lantern, and therefore the intensity of the lamp.
A small wooden box with a heavy door and various bolts and locks used to simulate slamming and other door sound effects offstage.
A light from directly above the acting area.
System of pipes arranged at the top of a safety curtain to drench it with water in the event of fire.
Tape or material used to cover the seams between flats, prior to painting.
Usually illuminated sign, of standard size, which should always be visible, showing an audience member and the company the nearest exit.

1) See Swag 2) Describes tabs which adopt a sculpted shape. 3) A length of cable incorporating a number of lamp holders used for outdoor party lighting etc. Available in multi-circuit form so that the lamps can be "chased".
A small box containing the socket into which a pyro cartridge is plugged. Also known as a flash pod.
Method of checking whether lanterns are functioning properly by flashing them on one at a time. It is good practice to flash lanterns to 70, rather than Full to preserve lamp life.
The metal bars to which scenery and lanterns are attached for flying above the stage.
igh working platform at the side(s) of the stage from which the flying l
The process of adjusting the direction and beam size of lanterns. Does not necessarily result in a "sharply focused" image.
Hydrous aluminium silicate, used in chemistry as a filter and as a binder when mixing powder paint for use on textiles.
Draperies made up with deep "gatherings" have fullness - usually requiring not less than 50 additional fabric, measured at head and foot.
A lamp with a revolving mirror and a coloured plastic dome. Gives a "police light" effect. Usually 12 Volt or 240 Volt operation.
A means for an actor to get off a rostrum, high level etc. out of view of the audience. Usually treads.

1) A long piece of scenery positioned at the base of a backcloth usually to mask the very bottom of a cloth or lanterns lighting a cloth. 2) Compartmentalised floodlight battens at floor level used to light the bottom of skycloths etc.
Usually refers to microphone/headset communications equipment. Abbreviated to "comms". Also known as "cans".
An array of jack sockets ("jills"), providing connections to equipment/outlets etc. A patch panel.

A type of animation disk which fits into the colour runners at the front of a lantern which rotates and breaks up the light beam to make it appear to be moving. Best used on a profile lantern containing a gobo.
Text of opera, or other long musical vocal composition. The script of a musical.

A flexible 3 ply timber, used for cladding flats etc. Also known as Philippine mahogany. Use is declining due to the fact that it is sourced from environmentally unsustainable resources in the Brazilian Rainforest.
A short stick used by scenic painters to steady the hand by resting its padded end against the surface being painted.
Wheeled rack for transporting a number of pre-rigged six-lamp bars or lanterns.
Lighting effect. A large shallow circular box with calico on one face and low wattage lamps arranged on the back. Can be flown behind a gauze or thin cyclorama to give the effect of the moon rising.

A flexible electrical cable composed of several well-insulated cores covered in a strong PVC or rubber covering. Enables a number of different circuits to be carried down one piece of cable. Both lighting and sound multicores are available.
Theatre or concert sound engineer. Normally male. But not exclusively so ! See also Techie and Lampy.
Connecting more than one lantern to one power outlet via an adaptor or splitter, or more than one speaker to one amplifier channel.
1) The folding frame that forms the base of a readily portable platform. 2) The opposite of SERIES when referring to wiring two loads into one outlet.
Dimmer levels are expressed as a percentage of the supply voltage. (100 = 240 Volts(UK)).
Lighting positions (often on platforms) at each side of the stage, immediately behind the proscenium.
Greek term for three-sided flats mounted on a rotating base. Used in rows to produce easily changed backings.
Hinge with removable pin used to join two pieces of scenery together (ie one half of the hinge is on each piece of scenery).

1) A lantern focused very tightly on a small area (eg an actors head) 2) A luminaire used widely in disco installations, consisting of a low voltage Par 36 lamp with a fine beam in a metal case with built in transformer.
The part of a computerised lighting control desk which enables the operator to recall cues from the electronic memory.
Smoother lighting builds from zero are achieved when a lamp filament has been warmed (at approx 15) in the previous state.
A function on some memory lighting control desks with video mimics. Preview enables the operator to see the levels of dimmers and other information in a lighting state other than that on stage.
The task, usually performed by stage management, of going around finding / borrowing / buying props for the production.
The department in the theatre whose job it is to entice the audience into the theatre, and to tell them what they need to know in order to get the most from the production.

A facility on multitrack recorders which allows you to "drop in" a sound onto a track whilst playing through the tape, sometimes controlled by a footswitch. Useful for correcting mistakes in an already recorded tape.
A box or tray containing dried peas etc which produces a rain sound effect when inclined.
A modification that can be made to an existing piece of equipment after purchase to bring it up to date.

A turntable built into the stage floor on which scenery can be set and then driven into view. Can be electrically chain driven, or manually pushed into position. A revolve can also be built on top of an existing stage.
(plural ROSTRA) A portable platform, usually in the form of a collapsible hinged framework (Gate) with a separate top (Lid).

The technique of recording a sound digitally (translating the analogue audio waveform into a series of electrical ons and offs that can be manipulated by a computer) for subsequent processing, editing and playback.
Attached to an unused spot line to stop it running back through the pulleys, and to enable it to fly in without fouling adjacent equipment.
High-ceilinged storage area adjacent to the stage, sometimes used for building and storing flats and other scenery.
To reset technical systems to a particular point in the show in order to repeat a sequence or scene during rehearsals.
A piece of flat iron screwed to the bottom rail of a door flat which holds it together, and ensures that the flat doesn't warp. Invisible to the audience.
The first rehearsal between Opera singers and the orchestra. No attempt is made to act or move the production at this rehearsal.
A plastic or metal "S" hook used to hang tabs etc. A sprung catch prevents the hook becoming detached.
Chalked piece of string which, when stretched tight and "snapped" is used for marking straight lines on stage or on scenery as a painting aid.
A temporary line dropped from the grid to suspend something in an exact special position.
A warning given to technical staff by stage management that a cue is imminent. Technicians acknowledge by saying "Standing By".
That part of a speaker system designed to extend the low frequency range of the system.
Track for suspending and operating horizontally moving curtains. May be hand or winch operated.
A continuous loop of tape which produces an "everlasting" sound effect when played. Used for any long sound needed (eg rain, wind) without having to continuously repeat a short effect.
A rope used to hold adjacent flats together as one via cleats.
Narrow masking flats adjacent and sometimes at right angles to the proscenium arch.
The area directly below the trapped part of the stage. Used for accessing the traps.
Trade name for a range of "intelligent" moving lights.
AC System - A control system for an AC motor which has a single synchronous speed or two different synchronous speeds.
Brace Rod - Supports for the outer corners of the platform, each of which tie to upper portions of the stile.

Brake shoe - Moving member(s) of a brake, lined with friction material which, when in contact with the brake drum, holds the elevator at floor level. On some types of control, it will stop the elevator when power is removed from the hoist motor.
Cable Wrap - That amount of the drive sheave actually in contact
Crosshead - (1) The upper member of the car frame. (2) The traveling member of a selector.
Door Gibs - Devices at the bottom of horizontal sliding door panels, which stick into sill grooves and eliminate door panels swinging in or out.
Fishplate - A steel plate, which spans the joint where two lengths of guide rails in a stack meet.
Hall Call - A call registered at a landing button or fixture.
Hoist Rope - The wire ropes used to raise and lower an elevator car.
Rail Clips - Devices bolted to guide rail brackets to clamp rails firmly in place.
1 Against 2 To assert a belief that something will decrease "I'm bearish on the economy"
1 In favor of 2 To assert a belief that something will increase "I'm bullish on our sales"
1 To reduce 2 To slow to near zero 3 To spend very little "We must clamp down our expenses"
1 A consultant with an expertise who may or may not have better knowledge than almost any employee "Do we need a hired gun "
1 Use resources owned by the firm to produce a good or provide a service "It was in sourced because we had the people" See: Out sourced
1 A prospective employee with all the required skills 2 Older and more experienced workers 3 Retrained workers "The applicant is job ready "
1 During the next period of time 2 In the future "Our sales will grow over time "
1 A step taken before something happens "We can prevent this by being proactive "
1 The firing of employees and/or the use of less plant and equipment "Our office is experiencing some reductions" See: Layoff
1 Unable to fulfill a promise 2 To do the opposite of what was promised "They had to renege on that promise"
1 The firing of employees and/or the reduction of plant and equipment "The firm surplused several people" See: Layoff
1 The firing of employees and/or the reduction of plant and equipment with a minimum reduction in production "We need to trim costs"
1 Benefit 2 Help "Where is the value add in having purchasing's opinion?"
1 Opinion 2 Point of view "Give me your take "
A mineral, obtained largely from Cornwall, used by papermakers to obtain finish and consistency; also for coating art and chromo paper. Also called Kaolin.
A board made from waste paper used mainly in packaging, especially with a white liner and coating.
Materials unsuitable for papermaking, present in some raw materials and waste paper.
Hollow cylinder of wire gauze, which consolidates the wet web on the wire and may produce a watermark.
A term applied comprehensively to the many varieties of papers used for printing purposes.
a unit of volume often used in oil-reservoir analysis, equivalent to the volume (as of oil or water) necessary to cover 1 acre to a depth of 1 foot.

over. The term usually describes conditions of flow on one side of a piece of equipment as compared with conditions on the opposite side where a fluid is flowing (e.g., a pressure drop across a separator).
A hoist. a mechanism for lifting operated by a compressed air motor;
One of the two classes of organic petrochemicals the other is the aromatics (q.v.), The most important aliphatics are the gases, ethylene. Butylene, acetylene and propylene.
The bottom most ring of steel plates in the wall of an upright, cylindrical tank.
An instrument for measuring the specific gravity of liquids; a hydrometer (q.v.).
Refers to rocks/minerals which were formed or were generated in place.
To reduce the level of liquid in a well bore by bailing.
the failure of an anchor to hold in a soft bottom, instead pulling out with a large ball of mud on it.
a fishing accessory run above a bit or mill to recover small pieces of metal or junk in a well.
A well whose fluid is being lifted by rods and pump actuated by a walking beam (q.v.).

In early pipeline parlance, the joint of line pipe laid just before the break for lunch. When the bean joint was bucked in (q.v.) the pipe liners grabbed lunch buckets from the gang truck and found a comfortable place to cat.
An excavation dug beneath a pipeline to provide room for the use of tools by workers; a hole larger in diameter at the bottom than at the top.
a protective grill or cover for a belt and pulleys.
A wooden shed built to protect the wide belt that runs from the engine to the band wheel on a cable tool rig or an old beam pumping well. The belt hall extends from the engine house to the derrick.

a circular ring used to determine whether a bit is of the correct outside diameter. Often bit gauges are used to determine if the bit has been worn down to a diameter smaller than specifications allow; such a bit is termed undergauge.
a report on each bit used in an operation, listing its type, the amount of footage it drilled, and the nature of the formation penetrated.

(1)A term denoting residual oil oil used in ships' boilers or in large heating or generating plants bunkers. (2) Black-colored oil used or lubricating heavy, slow-moving machinery where the use of higher-grade lubes would be impractical.
a pipe, usually casing, with no perforations.
A line on the wellhead or blowout preventer stack through which gas pressure can be bled to prevent a threatened blowout.
an integral part of a blowout preventer, serving as the closing element. Its ends do not fit around the drill pipe but seal against each other and shut off the space below completely. (See ram.)
a pumping device capable of transferring liquid; used to transfer crude oil and water mixtures if pump agitation would create unwanted emulsions.
An inexperienced worker or "green hand" on a drilling crew.
the steel projections on a crane that the boom strikes if raised too high or lowered too far.
a complete trip from the bottom of the wellbore to the top.

to begin operating 24 hours a day. Moving the rig and rigging up are usually carried on during daylight. When the rig is ready for operation on a new location, crews break tour and start operating 24 hours a day.
a metal cap that has openings allowing vapor bubbles in a gas-processing tower to contact cool liquids, causing some of the vapor to condense to liquid.
(slang) a large fan installed on a drilling rig to blow insects away from the work area; any type of fan.
A distribution point for petroleum products. A bulk plant usually has tank carunloading facilitiese and warehousing for products sold in packages or in barrels.
Common laborers who do the ditching and other heavy work on a pipeline construction job.
the large, circular gear in a mud pump that is driven by the prime mover and in turn drives the connecting rods.
a threaded nipple with a rounded, closed end, used to stop up a hole or close off the end of a line.
Said of a fishing toot lowered into the well bore that has latched onto lost pipe or another object being fished out and won't unlatch or cannot be disengaged. owing to a malfunction of the tool.
On a cable-tool rig, the large wheels and axle located on one side of the derrick floor used to hold the drilling line. See Calf Wheel.

(See jar.) bumper sub a device similar to ajar, but used in the normal drilling stem to compensate for vertical movement of the stem, especially in offshore drilling. It also provides jarring action, but to a lesser extent than a jar.
To supply fuel to vessels for use in the ships 'boilers; the loading of bunker fuel on board ship for use by the ship's boilers.

Crew quarters. usually a portable building used on remote well location to house the drilling crew and for supplies; quarters for Single 011 field workers in the days when transportation to a nearby town was unavailable.
a type of rotary shoe designed to mill away metal tubular goods (such as casing, drill pipe, and so on) causing stuck pipe; used in fishing operations.
a drilling bit with tungsten carbide inserts that resemble buttons. (See roller-cone bit.)
A cast-iron plug; a flat plug used to close the end of a pipe or a valve.

a chemical combination of calcium, carbon, and oxygen, the main constituent of limestone. It forms a tenacious scale in water-handling facilities and is a cause of water hardness. Chemical symbol is CaCO2.
pertaining to an independent leg jackup rig designed so that the legs may be slanted outward to increase support against lateral stresses when the unit is on the seafloor.
to control a blowout by placing a very strong valve on the wellhead.
a wellbore in which casing has been run.
A large refinery vessel for processing reduced crude oil, naphthas, or other intermediates in the presence of a catalyst. See Fluid Catalytic Cracking Unit.
he creation of a partial vacuum or a cavity by a high-speed blade or boat propeller
the middle line of the hull of a mobile offshore drilling rig from stem to stern as shown in a waterline view.
a processing network used to treat emulsion produced from several leases, thus eliminating the need for individual treating facilities at each lease site.
An early-day, square, box-like refining vessel; a still to heat crude oil for distilling the products in those days-kerosene, gas oil, and lubricating oil.
an extension of pipe from the blowout-preventer assembly, used to direct well fluids from the annulus to the choke manifold.
The measuring point at which a gas distributing utility receives gas from a gas transmission company.
Crude oil containing less than one percent sediment and water (BS&W) pipeline oil oil clean enough to be accepted by a pipeline for transmission.
To flatten the end of a pipe with a hydraulically powered set of pinchers. Pinching the pipe end is done to make a quick, temporary closure in the event a loaded pipeline is accidentally ruptured.
A lever and lengths of chain with hooks attached to the ends of the chains; used for tightening or pulling a chain. The hooks are alternately moved forward on the chain being tightened.
a manually operated device used to tighten guy wires or move heavy loads.
A seagoing vessel for drilling core holes in offshore areas.

to drill shallow, small-diameter wells to obtain geological information, usually in the bottom of an existing wellbore. A continuous sample of the formation is provided from the top to the final depth. See also sidewall coring.
abbr computerized production control. (see computer control)
the housing that encloses the crankshaft of an engine.
the driller or head well puller in charge on a well-servicing rig employed to pull sucker rods or tubing.
A person responsible for cleaning and keeping an oil field bunkhouse supplied with towels, bed linen, and soap, a construction camp housekeeper.
To shovel out the loose earth in the bottom of a ditch; also to square up the floor and side of the ditch in preparation for laying of pipe.

A unit of measurement for volume. It represents a volume one foot long, by one foot wide, by one foot deep. Natural gas is measured in cubic feet, but the measurements are usually expressed in terms of Bcf, Tcf, Mcf, or Quads.
Originally, a grease used in compression cups (q.v.) but today the term refers to grease having a calcium fatty-acid soap base. See Grease.
a powerful, high-explosive material (cyclo-trimethylene-trinitramine) used as the main charge in jet perforating guns; also called RDX. (See jet-perforate.)
A well that will not flow, and in order to produce must be put on the pump.

A pulley or sheave mounted in a steel frame which is securely fixed to the metal deck of a ship or barge. Deck blocks which lie horizontal to the vessel's deck are for horizontal pulls with hawser or cable.
to resolve an emulsion, especially of water and oil, into its components. (See emulsion treating.)

The charge incurred by the shipper for detaining a vessel, freight car, or truck. High loading rates for oil tankers are of utmost importance in order to speed turnaround and minimize demurrage charges.
the depth of the wellbore when a bit is pulled out of the hole. (See depth In.)
A member of the drilling crew who works up in derrick on the tubing board, racking tubing or drillpipe as it is pulled from the well and unscrewed by other crow members on the derrick floor.
a device similar to a die collar but with external threads.
Colloquial term used in the early days to describe small tracts, 1120 of an acre, just large enough to accommodate an oil derrick. The concept of pooling (q.v.) had not yet been accepted.
a plate at the base of a tank shell or wall that is removed to allow the tank tone cleaned.
A pipe in which the flow of liquid or gas is downward.

A type of large excavating machine made with a long boom over which a line runs down to a clamshell bucket. The bucket at the end of the fine is swung into position and is then dragged into the material to be moved or dug out.
the first U.S. well drilled in search of oil. Some 69 feet deep, it was drilled near Titusville, Pa., and completed in 1859.
the hoisting mechanism on a drilling rig. It is essentially a large winch that spools off or takes in the drilling line and thus raises or lowers the drill stem and bit.
to remove with the bit the residual cement that normally remains in the lower section of casing and the wellbore after the casing has been cemented.
the heavy seamless tubing used to rotate the bit and circulate the drilling fluid. joints of pipe 30 ft long are coupled together by means of tool joints.
the entire length of tubular pipes, composed of the kelly, the drill pipe, and drill collars, that make up the drilling assembly from the surface to the bottom of the hole.
pertaining to packers and other tools left in the wellbore to be broken up later by the drill bit. Drillable equipment is made of cast iron, aluminum, plastic, or other soft brittle material.

A self-propelled vessel, a ship equipped with a derrick amidships for drilling wells in deep water. A drillship is self-contained, carrying all of the supplies and equipment needed to drill and complete a well.
The drillpipe. In rotary drifting, the bit is attached to the drillstem or drift column which rotates to "dig" the hole.

A metal casing driven into the borehole of a well to prevent caving of the walls and to shut off surface water. The drive pipe, first used in an oil well by Colonel Drake, was the forerunner of the modern 'conductor or surface pipe. See Casing.
the drill pipe from which drilling mud has been emptied as it is pulled out of the wellbore.
a liquid-measuring device consisting of a small tank with narrowed sections at top and bottom that automatically fills and empties itself and records the number of dumps.
a calibrated metering tank designed to automatically release an accurate volume of liquid; also called a measuring tank.

a downhole motor driven by drilling fluid that imparts rotary motion to a drilling bit connected to the tool, thus eliminating the need to turn the entire drill stem to make hole. The Dyna-Drill, a trade name, is used in straight and directional drilling.
a well on the outer fringes of a productive subsurface formation.
the water that touches the edge of the oil in the lower horizon of a formation.
electric log; used in drilling reports. (See electric well log.)
a set of clamps that grip a stand, or column, of casing, tubing, drill pipe, or sucker rods, so that the stand can be raised or lowered into the hole.
A well in an area where petroleum has not been previously found or one targeted for formations above or below known reservoirs.
a fitting or device used to maintain or alter the direction of a rope or chain so that it leads directly to a sheave or drum without causing undue friction.
an oil company supervisor who controls production activities within a limited area.
the end of the drilling line that is affixed to the drum or reel of the drawworks, so called because it travels with greater velocity than any other portion of the line.
a subsurface hydrocarbon trap created by faulting, which causes an impermeable rock layer to be moved opposite the reservoir bed.
a pump installed in a field to transfer oil from a lease tank to a central gathering station near a main pipeline.
the temperature at which a petroleum product burns continuously after being ignited. (See flash point.)
Describes an item of equipment used in or over the well's borehole without parts-screws, lugs, wedges or dogs-that can come loose, tall into the well, and have to be fished out. See Captured Bolt
1. to use. flanges to make final connections on a piping system. 2. (slang) to complete any operation as, "They flanged up the meeting and went home."
To vaporize from heated charge stock; to distill.
a premature thickening or setting of cement slurry that makes it unpumpable.

a device that provides a flexible connection between the riser pipe and the subsea blowout preventers. By accommodating lateral movement of a mobile offshore drilling rig, flex joints help to prevent a buildup of abnormal bending load pressure.

a short, heavy, cylindrical steel section with a rounded bottom, attached to the bottom of the casing string. It contains a check valve and functions similarly to the float collar but also serves as a guide shoe for the casing.
Members-of the drilling crew (usually two) who work on the derrick floor.
A drilled plug in the flow line at the wellhead that controls the oil flow to desired rate. Flow beans are drilled with different-sized holes for different flow rates.
Subsea pipeline connecting satellite wells and/or platforms to a central production platform.
A diagrammatic drawing showing the sequence of refining or manufacturing operations in a plant.
A single unit that acts as an oil and gas separator, an oil heater, and an oil and water treater.
The distance between the wellhead and the point to which the fluid rises in the well.
A unit of energy or work equal to the work done in raising one pound the height of one foot against the force of gravity.
A type of check valve (q.v.) used on the "fool" or lower end of a suction pipe riser to maintain the column of liquid in the riser when the liquid is being drawn upward by a pump.
in the direction of the bow on offshore drilling rigs.
An interest in a well's oil and gas production free of any expense of that production; a royalty interest.
the water produced with oil. It usually settles out within rive minutes when the well fluids become stationary in a settling space within a vessel. Compare emulsified water.
An enclosure or a water pipe riser that is exposed to the weather, The freeze box or frost box surrounding the pips is filled with sawdust manure or other insulating materia1.
Designation for a valve, ran or other fitting whose opening is as large in cross section as the pipe, casing or tubing it is mounted on.

A light or medium-sized flat-bed truck carrying a portable doghouse or man rack where the pipeline repair crew rides to and from the job. The pipeliners toots are carried in compartments beneath the bed of the truck.
A drilling mud/gas separator, a surge chamber on the mud-flow line where entrained gas breaks out and is vented to a flare line; the gas-free mud is returned to the mud tanks or mud pits.

the use of the energy that arises from gas compressed in a reservoir to move crude oil to a wellbore. Gas drive is also used in a form of secondary recovery, in which gas is injected into input wells to sweep remaining oil to a producing well.
an installation in which natural gas is processed to prepare it for sale to consumers. A gas plant separates desirable hydrocarbon components from the impurities in natural gas.
A tank in which the production from a well or a lease is measured.
a cement or cement slurry that has been modified by the addition of bentonite.
(g)a unit of metric measure of mass and weight equal to 1/1,000 kg and nearly equal to 1 cm' of water at its maximum density.
The lowest, most powerful gear on a truck.
A knot tied in such a way as to defy untying an improperly tied square knot; ·hatchet knot.
A paraffin-base crude oil. Asphalt-base crudes are sometimes referred to as black oil.
a sand that contains considerable quantities of glauconite, a greenish mineral composed of potassium, iron, and silicate, which gives the sand its color and name.
(See temporary guide base and permanent guide base.)
A major submarine canyon indenting the seaward edge of the Scotian Shelf, which separates Banquereau and Sable Island Banks.
Rubber boots, the kind you pull on like a cowboy boot.
to suspend sucker rods in a derrick or mast on rod hangers rather than place them horizontally on a rack.
A warning cry given by a fellow worker when anything is accidentally dropped or fails from overhead toward another worker.

An electrical heating element made in the form of an insulated wire or tape used as a tracer line to provice heat to a pipeline or instrument piping. The heat tape is held in direct contact with the piping by a covering of insulation.
In refinery parlance, heavy ends are the heavier fractions of refined oil fuel oils, tubes, paraffin, and asphalt-remaining after the lighter fractions have been distilled off. See Light Ends.
a mechanical arrangement that prevents the upward movement of certain pieces of equipment installed in a well. A sucker-rod pump may use a mechanical hold-down for attachment to a seating nipple.
a series of beds dipping in the same direction.
A pulley or shrive mounted in wooden or metal frame to which a hook is attached. A hook block may have more than one sheave mounted in the frame a traveling block (q.v.).
the curved section on the oil-well end of the walking beam of a beampumping unit from which the bridle is suspended.

An old oil field term for unexplainable expense account items in the days of the teamster and line rider who were given an allowance for horse feed. Expenses that needed to be masked in anonymity were simply listed "horse feed."
the copyrighted name of a method of hydraulic fracturing to increase productivity.

to apply hydraulic pressure to check for leaks in tubing or tubing couplings, usually as the tubing is being run in the well. If water leaks from any place in the tubing, either the joint of tubing, the coupling, or both are replaced.

A substance that slows down a chemical reaction. An inhibitor's role is the reverse of a catalyst's. Inhibitors are sometimes used to interfere with a chemical reaction somewhere along the process train.
A well used for injecting water or gas into a formation in a secondary recovery or pressure maintenance operation.
a set of mounted blades (as the rotor of a centrifugal pump) used to impart motion to a fluid.
A high-octane blending stock for automotive gasoline.

a short shaft that is usually set between two machines to provide increased or decreased flexibility and speed.An intermediate; haft in the power train. Jack shafts usually are relatively short and often are splined.
a short rope used on the cathead of the drilling rig to tighten pipe-joints by pulling on the makeup longs.
to use a jet to clean out the cellar, slush pit, and so forth.
A metal housing that supports and protects a journal bearing. See Journal.
A technique used to enlarge an oil tanker's carrying capacity by cutting the vessel in two amidships and inserting a section between the halves.

A condition downhole when the drill collar or another part of the drillstring becomes wedged in a section of crooked hole, particularly a dogleg which is an abrupt deviation from the vertical or the general direction of the hole being drilled.
This symbol is used in petrophysical and reserves calculations to represent the maximum permeability of a rock formation.
a high-pressure line that connects the mud pump and the well and through which heavy drilling fluid can be pumped into the well to control a threatened blowout.
a printed form that contains blank spaces for recording information about killing an impending blowout, provided to remind personnel of the necessary steps to take to kill a well.
(See lease automatic custody transfer, and LACT.)
a barge used in the construction and placement of underwater pipelines. joints of pipe are welded together and then lowered off the stern of the barge as it moves ahead.
A bench on which workers, when not working, may rest. A perch from which a work operation may be observed by workers or loafers.
Lines through which production from individual wells is run to a tease tank battery.
(pronounced "leed") the pipe tongs suspended in the derrick and operated by a wireline connected to the breakout cathead. They are also called breakout tongs.
The more volatile products of petroleum refining e.g. butane, propane, gasoline.
a steel or plastic pipe used in pipelines, gathering systems, flow lines, and so forth.
the distance that a liner extends into the bottom of a string of casing.
to run any of the various logs used to ascertain downhole information about a well.
a daily report sheet on which operating data is entered by gaugers, dispatchers, and station engineers.
to deepen the hole made by the bit; to drill ahead.
To screw a pipe or threaded connection tight by the use of a wrench.
Petroleum found by wells offshore or on the continental shelf.
a distinctive, easily identified rock stratum, especially one used as a guide for drilling.
to obtain an accurate measurement of the depth reached in a well by measuring the drill pipe or tubing as it is run into the well.
a silicate mineral characterized by sheet cleavage. Biotite is ferromagnesian black mica, and muscovite is potassic white mica. Sometimes mica is used as a lost-circulation material in drilling.
A unit of permeability of a rock formation; one-thousandth of a darcy. See Darcy.
Cutting a "window" in a well's casing with a tool lowered into the hole on the drillstring.
A lever; a pry pole usually made by cutting a small tree; used on pipeline construction as an adjunct to the jack board and in lowering the pipeline into the ditch.
A small bailer used to retrieve cuttings from the bottom of a cable tool drilling well.
an employee of a mud-logging company who keeps the mud log.
a special form filled out by the mud man that records the properties of the drilling mud used while a well is being drilled.
Portable metal banks to hold drilling mud. Mud tanks are used where it is impractical to dig mud pits (q.v.) at the well site.
Measurement While Drilling. A technique to determine the real-time position of the drill bit in a directionally drilled well during the drilling process using instrumentation placed near the bit.
Gas originally in place in an underground formation as opposed to gas injected into the structure.
to bolt together various valves or fittings (as to nipple up the blowout preventers or the Christmas tree).

A sound detection system inside a logging tool designed to pick up vibrations caused by flowing liquid or gas downhole. The device is used to check the effectiveness of a squeeze job (q.v.), to estimate the gas flow from perforated formations, etc.

A device used by engineers and scientists for making rapid calculations; a graph that enables one, with the aid of a straightedge, to find the value of a dependent variable when the values of two or more independent variables are given.
A specially designed vessel for carrying ore and crude, both in bulk form. The first oil and bulk ore tanker/carrier was launched in 1966 and used in handling relatively small cargoes of oil and ore.
Another name for unloading; offloading refers more specifically to liquid cargo crude oil and refined products.
the surface area overlying an oil reservoir or reservoirs. Commonly, the term includes not only the surface area but may include the reservoir, the wells. and production equipment as well.

A form referring broadly to the oil field, to areas of exploration, production, and pipelining.

a gland arrangement that seals by pressure and is used to prevent leakage and waste of gas, oil, or water around a wireline (as when swabbing a well). It is operated either mechanically or hydraulically.
a representative of an oil company who gathers data on new oil and gas wells and other industry developments.
Term used for a processing plant, a refinery or a pumping station that is operating. To bring on stream is to start up a plant or an operation.
of a tank, open to pump suction.
any wellbore in which casing has not been set.
an excess quantity of fluid used to push acid out of the tubing or casing when an acid mixture is displaced into a well, thus directing the acid to the desired place in the well.

A type of junk mill (q.v.) with a tapered confer projection below the cutting surface of the bit to guide or pilot the bit into the open end of a piece of junk or a toot to be milled out downhole.

a packer in which the packing element is held in position by brass or steel pins. When weight is put on the packer, two metal sleeves telescope, shearing the pins and allowing the element to fold and pack off.
a geological structure that forms a trap for oil and gas when a porous and permeable rock ends at or stops against an impervious formation.
any device equipped with rollers and used to move drill pipe or collars.
a horizontal support for tubular goods.
a sealing component for a blowout preventer that closes the annular space between the pipe and the blowout preventer or wellhead.

A stirrup-like sling made of heavy belting material used on the winch line of boom cats for lifting, handling, and lowering in of pipe. Fabric slings are used to prevent scarring or damaging the pipelines protective coating.

One who does pipeline construction or repair work welders, ditching machine operators. cat drivers, costing and wrapping operators, connection men; broadly, anyone who is involved in the building, maintenance, and operation of a pipeline system.
1. a metal shaft that joins the piston to the crankshaft in an engine. 2. a metal shaft in a mud pump, one end of which is connected to the piston and the other to the pony rod.
Specially formulated plastic sheeting for lining earthen or leaking concrete pits to prevent seepage of oil or water into the ground.
A book containing maps of land plots arranged according to Township and Range for counties within a state. See Plat.

A catalytic reforming unit which converts low-quality straight-chain paraffins or naphthenes to low-boiling, branched-chain paraffins or aromatics of higher octane; a refinery unit that produces high-octane blending stock for manufacture of gasoline.

to place cement in or near the bottom of a well to exclude bottom water, sidetrack, or produce from a formation already drilled through. Plugging back also can be accomplished by a mechanical plug set by wireline, tubing, or drill pipe.
A type of quick-opening pipeline valve constructed with a central core or "plug." The valve can be opened or closed with one-quarter turn of the plug; a stop.

A plan for financing oil and gas exploration developed for off shore exploration. The form of the plan is usually corporate, the investors receiving shares of stock in the corporation and other securities.
a hydraulically powered device used to turn the drill pipe, tubing, or casing in a well in lieu of a rotary.

An air or hydraulically powered mechanism for making up and breaking out joints of drillpipe, casing or tubinq. After a joint is stabbed, the power tongs are latched onto the pipe which is screwed in and tightened to a predetermined torque.
the quantity of fluid used ahead of the acid solution pumped into a well in an acid-stimulation treatment; sometimes called spearhead. Compare overflush.

The parties proposing to carry out SOEP; specifically, Mobil Oil Canada Properties, Lead Operator, Shell Canada Limited, Joint Operator, Imperial Oil Resources Limited and Nova Scotia Resources Limited.
a building that houses the pumps, engines, and control panels at a pipeline gathering station or trunk station.
a surface unit similar to a pumping unit but having no individual power plant. Usually several pump jacks are operated by pull rods or cables from one central power source.
any of the valves on a reciprocating pump (as the suction and discharge valves) or on a sucker-rod pump (as a ball-and-scat valve). (See standing valve and traveling valve.)
a length of drill pipe, tubing, or casing shorter than 30 ft.
A specially refined oil with a high flash point (q.v.) Used in steel mills to cool hot metal.
1. To place pipe withdrawn from the hole on a pipe rack. 2. To stand pipe on the derrick floor when coming out of the hole.
In solvent-refining practice, raffinate is that portion of the oil being treated that remains undissolved and is not removed by the selective solvent.

A closure mechanism on well's blowout preventer stack fitted with chisel like jaws that are hydraulically operated. When the ram is closed on the Pipe the jaws or blades cut the pipe, permitting the upper section to be removed from the bop stack.
Kerosene-type product used in old kerosene stoves or cooking ranges.
a crude oil before it is refined.
a layer of sedimentary rock that is predominantly red, especially one of the permian or triassic age.
to increase or maintain reservoir pressure by injecting a pressurized fluid (as air, gas, or water) to effect greater ultimate recovery.
The "science" of divination by rods, wands. And switches. See doodle bug.
the area immediately around the rotary table and extending to each corner of the derrick or mast; the area immediately above the substructure on which the drawworks, rotary table, and so forth rest.
pl the metal parts (with the exceptions of nails, bolts, guy wires, and sand lines) used in the construction of the standard cable-tool rig.
A geologist; a humorous but affectionate colloquialism for a person who Assiduously pursues rock specimens in a search for evidence of oil and gas deposits.

a ratchet mechanism actuated by a fixed rod or chain connection with the walking beam of a pumping unit that provides a slow rate of rotation to the rod string, distributing the wear uniformly on both rods and tubing. (see sucker rod.)
The fee paid to a landowner for the easement of a pipeline right of way across his property. Right of way is measured in rods (16 1/2 feet) hence the term roddage fee. See right of way.
A rack with finger-like projections on which rods are hung when pulled from the well; a vertical rack for hanging lengths of pumping rods.
To agitate a trank of crude oil with air or gas for the purpose of mixing small quantities of chemical with the oil to break up emulsions or to settle out impurities.

The rock-cutting tool on the bottom of the drillstring made with three or four shanks welded together to form a tapered body. Each shank supports a cone-like wheel with case-hardened teeth that rotate on steel bearings.

A derrick equipped with rotary drilling equipment, i.e., Drilling engines. Draw works, rotary table, mud pumps, and auxiliary equipment; a modern Drilling unit capable of drilling a borehole with a bit attached to a rotating column of steel pipe.

Members of the drilling crew; the driller's assistants who work on the derrick floor, up in the derrick racking pipe, tend the drilling engines and mud Pumps, and on "trips" operate the pipe tongs breaking out or unscrewing the stands of drillpipe.
the action of pulling out and subsequently running back into the hole a string of drill pipe or tubing. It is also called tripping the pipe.
to transfer oil from a stock tank into a pipeline.
a platform encircling the top of the derrick.
a record of the oil transferred from the producer's storage tank to the pipeline. It is the basic legal instrument by which the lease operator is paid for oil produced and sold.
A classification of lubricating oils in terms of viscosity only. A standard established by the society of automotive engineers. Sae 20; sae 1ow. 30, multiviscosity lubricating oil (q.v.).

A small cotton bag with a drawstring to hold rock cutting samples. Each bag with its sample is tagged with identifying information, well name, lease, location, depth at which cuttings were taken, etc.

A sand or sandstone formation defined by upper and lower layers of impervious rock. Sandstone formation, sometimes in the shape of a lens, sandwiched between two impervious layers of rock; a geologic trap favorable to the accumulation of oil and gas.
a column of sand that has entered and accumulated in the wellbore.
a wire rope used on well-servicing rigs to operate a swab or bailer. It is usually 9/16 in. In diameter and several thousand feet long.
A cylinder with a plunger and valve arrangement used for sucking up the pulverized rock, sand, and water from the bottom of the well bore. More effective than a simple bailer. Shell pump; sludger.
a metal drum on a drilling rig or workover unit around which the sand line is wound.
1. Of a well, under restricted production because of sand accumulation in the wellbore. 2. Impeded or hindered, especially because of sand accumulation.
a device made up in the drill stem to absorb much of the wear between frequently broken joints (as the kelly and drill pipe.)
to run and cement casing at a certain depth in the wellbore; to set pipe.
the mud pit adjacent to the shale shaker, usually the first pit into which the mud flows after returning from the hole.

Oil obtained by treating the hydrocarbon kerogen found in certain kinds of shale deposits. When the shale is heated the resulting vapors are condensed and then treated in an involved process to form what is called shale oil or synthetic oil.
The shot hole (q.v.), The point at which a detonation is to be made in a geophysical survey.
a heavy weight or bar placed on or near a lightweight wireline tool. It provides weight so that the tool can be lowered into the well properly.
A product-dispensing tank mounted on skids or runners. Can be pulled or carried on a truck.
A metal patch made out of a section of pipe welded over a pitted or corroded section of pipeline. See half sole.
Rope made of hemp, sisal. Jute, or nylon, as distinguished from wire rope which is a steel cable.

The name of the gusher brought in by capt. Anthony lucas, near beaumont, texas, in 1902. The well, the first important producer ever drilled with Rotary tools, blew in (literary) and produced, at the rate of 75.000 to 100,0000 barrels day.
A type of lean oil (q.v.) Used in refinery absorber columns to absorb light petroleum fractions or a fighter lean oil that has vaporized in an upstream process.
an oil pipeline that picks up oil from the gathering lines of several oil fields and delivers it to a main line or trunk line.

A small charge of nitroglycerin set off in the bottom of a well as part of a workover operation after cleaning out a well, freeing the producing interval of sand and silt, a small explosive charge may be set of,' to 'wake up the well."
Seconds saybolf universal and seconds saybolt furol (q.v.).

A device on a steam line designed to trap air and water condensate and automatically bleed the air and drain the water from the system with a minimum loss of steam pressure.
Refers to the artificial "reels" fromed by the substructures of offshore drilling and production platforms that attract a variety of marine life from barnacles and algae to many kinds of fish.
A preprinted lease form (bought at the store) with blanks to be filled in by the parties to the lease.
A fight fuel oil or kerosene used in certain kinds of wickless-burner stoves.
a well that is drilled primarily to obtain geological information and that is usually not completed even if commercial quantities of petroleum are found.
to thread the drilling line through the sheaves of the crown block and traveling block. One end of the line is secured to the hoisting drum and the other to the derrick substructure.
1. To remove the drill stem from the hole while the blowout preventers are closed. 2. To pull the drill stem and the washover pipe out of the hole at the same time.
An auxiliary fine attached to an existing fine by use of a tap saddle (q.v.) Or by welding on a nipple or other fitting.

drill pipe, drill collars, casing, or tubing that has inadvertently become lodged immovably in the hole. It may occur when drilling is in progress, when casing is being run in the hole, or when the drill pipe is being hoisted.
Steel rods that are screwed together to form a "string" that connects the pump inside a well's tubing downhole to the pumping jack on the surface; pumping rods.
A screw-end pipeline plug a pipeline fitting one end of which is closed and tapered to resemble a bull's nose; a nipple-like fitting, one end threaded, the other end closed.
A terminal or oil-handling facility located offshore in water deep enough to accommodate the largest, deep-draft oil tankers.

A vessel on a flow line whose function is to receive and neutralize sudden, transient rises or surges in the stream of liquid. Surge tanks often are used on systems where fluids flow by heads (q.v.) Owing to entrained gas.
The diagonal support braces on a rig structure. Along with the horizontal girts, sway braces hold the legs (the corner members) of the rig in place.
Natural gas free of significant amounts of hydrogen sulfide (h2s) when produced.
Crude oil containing very little sulfur and having a good odor.
Spot weld temporarily joining two joints of pipe to hold them in position for complete welding.

a table giving the barrels of fluid contained in a storage tank corresponding to the linear measurement on a gauge line. Tank tables are prepared from tank strapping measurements. (See strap.)
a fishing tool that is run into a hollow fish (as a drill collar) and rotated to cut sufficient threads to provide a firm grip, permitting the fish to be pulled and recovered.

Heavy-duty, threaded joints specially designed to couple and uncouple drillpipe into "stands" (q.v.) of such length that they can be racked in the derrick. intermediate couplings between the tool joints are made with regular pipe collars.

A record book maintained by the district land offices of the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), listing all entries affecting described land.

a metal plate through which the tubes in the tube bundles are placed for support, effecting a pressure-tight connection between the tubes and the heads of a condenser or heat exchanger.
A weld or flanged fitting in the shape of a U used in construction of manifolds, exchanger bundles, and other close pipe work.
the act of pulling tubing out of and running it back into a well.
A link with a screw thread at one end and a swivel at the other; a right-and left screw link used for tightening a rod, a guy wire, or stay.
of drill pipe or drill collars, to part or split primarily because of metal fatigue in the pipe or because of mishandling.

cavities in a rock that do not contain solid material but may contain fluids.
a tank containing heated water,Through which crude-oil emulsion is forced to flow, used to remove the water from the crude. It is also called a gun barrel.

the portion of an oil or gas reservoir occupied by water, usually the lowest zone in the reservoir.
to increase the specific gravity, or density, of the drilling fluid by adding weighting material.
